qna.a: No. SELF JOIN describes joining a table to itself. The actual join can use INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, or another supported join type.

qna.q: Q9. What is an important risk when comparing rows with a SELF JOIN?
qna.a: You can produce duplicate or reverse pairs, and the number of rows can grow quickly depending on the join condition.

qna.q: Q10. Why is SELF JOIN useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It is useful for transforming parent-child relationships, enriching hierarchical data, comparing records within the same dataset, and preparing data for downstream reporting or pipelines.

items.title: Join Multiple Tables
explanation: What Does Joining Multiple Tables Mean?

In real-world databases, information is usually distributed across multiple related tables. Joining multiple tables means combining data from three or more tables in a single SQL query using relationships between their columns.
Data Engineering frequently requires this because source data is often normalized across separate tables such as customers, orders, products, stores, and payments.
Definition: Joining multiple tables means connecting three or more tables through their related columns so that information from all required tables can be returned in one result.
Why Do We Join Multiple Tables?
Suppose an order system stores information like this:

customers
---------
customer_id
customer_name

orders
------
order_id
customer_id
product_id

products
--------
product_id
product_name
price
No single table contains all the information required for a report.
If we want to answer:
Which customer ordered which product and what was its price?
we need to connect all three tables.
Example Table Relationships

customers
    |
    | customer_id
    ↓
 orders
    |
    | product_id
    ↓
products

customers → orders → products
The relationships form a chain. SQL can follow that chain and combine the required information.
Basic Syntax

SELECT
    ...
FROM table1 t1
JOIN table2 t2
    ON t1.key = t2.key
JOIN table3 t3
    ON t2.key = t3.key;
The important idea is that each additional JOIN connects another table to the result using an appropriate relationship.
Joining Three Tables
Consider these tables:
We can join all three tables:

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    p.price
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
Possible result:

customer_name | order_id | product_name | price
--------------|----------|--------------|------
John          | 101      | Laptop       | 50000
Alice         | 102      | Keyboard     | 2000
John          | 103      | Keyboard     | 2000
How SQL Processes the JOIN Chain
You can think about the query as progressively building a result:

Step 1:
customers
    +
orders
    ↓
customer + order information

Step 2:
customer + order information
    +
products
    ↓
customer + order + product information
The database optimizer may execute the joins in a different physical order for performance, but logically you should understand the query as connecting the related tables through their keys.
Joining Four or More Tables
You can continue adding JOIN clauses when more tables are required.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    s.store_name,
    pay.payment_method
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN stores s
    ON o.store_id = s.store_id
JOIN payments pay
    ON o.order_id = pay.order_id;
There is no fixed limit of three tables. The number of tables depends on the data model and the information required by the query.
Using Different JOIN Types Together
Multiple-table queries do not have to use the same JOIN type for every table.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    pay.payment_method
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN payments pay
    ON o.order_id = pay.order_id;
This can preserve customers even when they do not have orders, products, or payments.
INNER JOIN Across Multiple Tables
If all joins are INNER JOINs, a row normally remains in the final result only when the required relationship exists through every join.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
If an order references a product that has no matching product row, that order will not appear in this result.
LEFT JOIN Across Multiple Tables
LEFT JOIN is useful when the first table represents the records you must preserve.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
For example, a customer with no orders can still appear with NULL values for order and product columns.
Important: Choose the Correct Join Path
Before writing a multiple-table query, understand how the tables are related.

customers.customer_id
        ↓
orders.customer_id

orders.product_id
        ↓
products.product_id
Do not randomly join columns just because their data types look similar. The join condition should represent a real business relationship.
Rule: Before joining multiple tables, identify the primary key, foreign key, and grain of each table. Then determine the correct relationship between them.
Joining Multiple Tables with Aliases
Aliases become increasingly important as the number of tables increases.

FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
Instead of repeatedly writing long table names, aliases make the query shorter and easier to read.
Multiple Tables and Duplicate Rows
Joining multiple tables can unexpectedly increase the number of rows.
For example, suppose one customer has three orders:

1 customer
    ↓
3 orders
    ↓
3 result rows
If an order has multiple payment records, joining payments can increase the rows further:

1 customer
    ↓
3 orders
    ↓
6 payment records
    ↓
6 joined rows
The exact multiplication depends on the cardinality of each relationship.
One-to-Many Relationships
A common relationship is one-to-many.

Customer
   |
   ├── Order 1
   ├── Order 2
   └── Order 3
When you join the customer table with orders, the customer information can appear multiple times because there are multiple matching orders.
Many-to-Many Relationships
Many-to-many relationships usually involve a bridge or junction table.

students
   |
   | student_id
   ↓
enrollments
   ↑
   | course_id
   |
courses
For example:

SELECT
    s.student_name,
    c.course_name
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e
    ON s.student_id = e.student_id
JOIN courses c
    ON e.course_id = c.course_id;
The bridge table connects students and courses.
Filtering After Multiple JOINs
You can use WHERE after joining multiple tables to filter the final row-level result.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE p.price > 10000;
This returns joined records where the product price is greater than 10,000.
Aggregating After Multiple JOINs
Multiple-table joins are frequently followed by GROUP BY for Data Engineering and analytics.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count,
    SUM(p.price) AS total_value
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name;
However, be careful: if additional one-to-many tables are joined before aggregation, the joins can multiply rows and produce incorrect totals. Always verify the grain before aggregating.
Join Multiple Tables in Data Engineering
This pattern is extremely common in ETL and analytics pipelines.

orders
   +
customers
   +
products
   +
stores
   ↓
Enriched Dataset
   ↓
Transformation
   ↓
Data Warehouse / Data Lake
   ↓
Reporting / Analytics
For example, an ETL pipeline might combine raw order data with customer, product, and store reference data before loading an analytical table.
Common Mistakes

• Joining tables using unrelated columns.
  • Forgetting a JOIN condition and accidentally creating a Cartesian product.
  • Using the wrong JOIN type and losing required records.
  • Not understanding one-to-many or many-to-many relationships.
  • Aggregating after a row-multiplying join without checking the grain.
  • Using SELECT * when many tables contain similarly named columns.
  • Using unclear aliases in a query with many tables.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide duplicate rows caused by an incorrect join.
Best Practice for Multiple-Table Queries

1. Understand the purpose and grain of each table.
  2. Identify primary and foreign keys.
  3. Draw the relationship between tables before writing the query.
  4. Start with the main table.
  5. Add one JOIN at a time.
  6. Check the row count after each JOIN.
  7. Only then add filters and aggregations.

Data Engineering Rule: When debugging a complex JOIN query, add the tables one at a time and check the row count after each JOIN. If the row count suddenly increases unexpectedly, investigate that relationship before continuing.
Quick Summary

• Multiple-table JOINs combine data from three or more related tables.
  • Each JOIN normally needs a relationship expressed through an ON condition.
  • Different JOIN types can be combined in the same query.
  • Aliases make multiple-table queries easier to read.
  • One-to-many and many-to-many relationships can increase result rows.
  • Always understand table grain before using aggregates.
  • Multiple-table joins are fundamental to ETL, reporting, and data warehouse transformations.
practice: Step 1: Create three tables representing customers, orders, and products.

customers
customer_id | customer_name
------------|--------------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob

orders
order_id | customer_id | product_id
---------|-------------|-----------
101      | 1           | 10
102      | 2           | 20
103      | 1           | 20

products
product_id | product_name | price
-----------|--------------|------
10         | Laptop       | 50000
20         | Keyboard     | 2000
Step 2: Join customers and orders and display the customer name with the order ID.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Step 3: Add the products table and display customer name, order ID, product name, and price.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    p.price
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
Step 4: Change the query to LEFT JOINs so that customers without orders are also displayed.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id;
Step 5: Add a WHERE condition to return only products costing more than 10,000.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    p.price
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE p.price > 10000;
Step 6: Add a fourth table such as stores and join it using store_id from the orders table.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    p.product_name,
    s.store_name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN stores s
    ON o.store_id = s.store_id;
Step 7: Before adding an aggregate function, check how many rows each JOIN produces. Identify whether each relationship is one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.
Step 8: Build an analytical query that shows each customer and the number of orders they placed.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name;

Practice Goal: You should be able to join three or more related tables, choose the correct JOIN type, understand how relationships affect row counts, and safely build multi-table queries for Data Engineering tasks.

qna.q: Q1. What does joining multiple tables mean?
qna.a: It means combining data from three or more related tables in a single SQL query.

qna.q: Q2. How do you join three tables?
qna.a: Start with one table, join the second table using an ON condition, and then add another JOIN with the appropriate relationship to the third table.

qna.q: Q3. Can different JOIN types be used in the same query?
qna.a: Yes. A query can combine INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, and other supported join types depending on the required result.

qna.q: Q4. Why are aliases important when joining multiple tables?
qna.a: Aliases make queries shorter and clearer and help distinguish columns when multiple tables contain columns with the same names.

qna.q: Q5. What happens when a one-to-many relationship is joined?
qna.a: The row from the one side can appear multiple times, once for each matching row on the many side.

qna.q: Q6. Why can a many-to-many relationship be dangerous?
qna.a: It can produce a large number of rows and may multiply records unexpectedly if the relationship is not understood.

qna.q: Q7. Why should table grain be understood before aggregation?
qna.a: Because joins can multiply rows. If aggregation is performed after unexpected row multiplication, totals and counts can become incorrect.

qna.q: Q8. How should you debug a complex multiple-table JOIN?
qna.a: Add one JOIN at a time and check the result and row count after each JOIN. This helps identify where unexpected rows are introduced.

qna.q: Q9. What is a common mistake when joining multiple tables?
qna.a: Joining unrelated columns, missing a JOIN condition, choosing the wrong JOIN type, or using DISTINCT to hide an incorrect join.

qna.q: Q10. Why are multiple-table JOINs important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data pipelines frequently combine data from operational tables, reference tables, customer data, product data, and other sources to create enriched datasets for warehouses, analytics, and reporting.

items.title: `ON` vs `WHERE` in JOINs
explanation: Why `ON` vs `WHERE` Matters
When writing JOIN queries, both ON and WHERE can contain conditions, but they serve different purposes.
ON primarily defines how rows from two tables are matched, while WHERE filters rows from the result of the query.
Simple Rule: Use ON to define the relationship between joined tables. Use WHERE to filter the rows you want in the final result.
Basic Example

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_name = 'John';
Here:

• ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id determines which customer row matches which order row.
  • WHERE c.customer_name = 'John' filters the joined result to John.
Think of Them as Two Different Questions

ON
↓
"How should these tables be related?"

WHERE
↓
"Which rows from the result do I want?"
`ON` Defines the JOIN Relationship
The most common JOIN condition uses a primary key and foreign key.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
The ON condition says that a customer and an order should be matched when their customer_id values are equal.
`WHERE` Filters the Result

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id > 100;
The JOIN first establishes the customer-order relationship, and the WHERE condition filters the resulting rows.
Very Important Difference with INNER JOIN
With an INNER JOIN, moving some conditions between ON and WHERE can produce the same final result.

-- Query 1
SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id > 100;

-- Query 2
SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.order_id > 100;
For an INNER JOIN, these commonly produce the same matching rows because unmatched rows are removed by the INNER JOIN anyway.
Important: Although conditions may sometimes be moved between ON and WHERE with INNER JOINs without changing the result, this does not mean they are interchangeable in all JOINs.
The Critical Difference with LEFT JOIN
The difference becomes very important when using an OUTER JOIN, especially LEFT JOIN.
Consider:

customers
-------------------------
customer_id | name
-------------------------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob

orders
-------------------------
order_id | customer_id | status
-----------------------------------
101      | 1           | PAID
102      | 1           | CANCELLED
103      | 2           | PAID
Suppose we want all customers, but only their PAID orders.
Condition in `ON`

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID';
Result:

name  | order_id | status
------|----------|--------
John  | 101      | PAID
Alice | 103      | PAID
Bob   | NULL     | NULL
The condition in ON controls which orders are allowed to match each customer. Customers without a matching PAID order are still preserved because this is a LEFT JOIN.
Condition in `WHERE`

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
Result:

name  | order_id | status
------|----------|--------
John  | 101      | PAID
Alice | 103      | PAID
Bob disappears because the LEFT JOIN initially gives Bob NULL values for the order columns. The WHERE o.status = 'PAID' condition then rejects the NULL row.

LEFT JOIN + condition in ON

Customers
   ↓
Keep ALL customers
   ↓
Only matching PAID orders
   ↓
Customers without PAID orders remain

LEFT JOIN + condition in WHERE

Customers
   ↓
LEFT JOIN creates NULL for missing orders
   ↓
WHERE status = 'PAID'
   ↓
NULL rows are removed
   ↓
Effectively behaves like an INNER-style filter
Side-by-Side Comparison

Condition LocationMain PurposeLEFT JOIN Effect
ONControls which right-side rows matchUnmatched left rows can still remain
WHEREFilters the joined resultCan remove rows created with NULL right-side values
Filtering the Left Table
A condition on the left table can also be placed in different locations, but the effect is important for outer joins.

-- Filter customers before/while determining the match
SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND c.name <> 'Bob';
Bob is still present because the LEFT JOIN preserves the left-side row, but Bob will not match an order through that condition.

-- Filter the final result
SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.name <> 'Bob';
Here Bob is removed from the final result because WHERE filters the final rows.
Multiple Conditions in `ON`
The ON clause can contain multiple conditions.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID'
   AND o.order_id > 100;
All conditions in the ON clause determine whether the right-side row matches.
Multiple Conditions in `WHERE`
The WHERE clause can also contain multiple filtering conditions.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
  AND o.order_id > 100;
These conditions filter the rows returned by the query.
`ON` Does Not Mean "Only for JOIN Keys"
A common beginner misconception is that ON can contain only equality between primary and foreign keys.
That is not true. Additional matching conditions can be included.

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID';
The key relationship and additional matching conditions can both be expressed in ON.
Data Engineering Example
Suppose a pipeline needs every product and only its currently active inventory records.

SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    i.quantity
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN inventory i
    ON p.product_id = i.product_id
   AND i.status = 'ACTIVE';
This keeps products that have no active inventory record. Their inventory columns become NULL.
If the condition were placed in WHERE:

SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    i.quantity
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN inventory i
    ON p.product_id = i.product_id
WHERE i.status = 'ACTIVE';
Products without an inventory match would be removed. That may be incorrect if the business requirement is to keep every product.
Common Mistake: Accidentally Turning LEFT JOIN into INNER JOIN

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
This is a common mistake when the intention was to preserve all customers. The WHERE condition rejects rows where o.status is NULL.
If you want all customers and only PAID orders, put the order filter in the ON clause:

SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID';
Practical Decision Rule

Ask yourself:

1. Is this condition defining which rows should MATCH?
       ↓
      ON

2. Is this condition filtering rows I want in the FINAL RESULT?
       ↓
     WHERE
Important Note About Query Execution

For learning purposes, think of JOIN matching as being controlled by ON and final row filtering as being controlled by WHERE. The database optimizer may physically execute operations in a different order while producing the same correct result.
Common Mistakes

• Putting a right-table filter in WHERE when a LEFT JOIN is supposed to preserve unmatched left rows.
  • Assuming ON and WHERE are always interchangeable.
  • Using WHERE conditions that accidentally eliminate NULL-extended rows from an outer join.
  • Using JOIN conditions that do not represent the actual relationship between tables.
  • Moving conditions without checking how the JOIN type affects the result.
Quick Summary

• ON defines which rows from joined tables match.
  • WHERE filters rows from the query result.
  • With INNER JOIN, some conditions can often be placed in either location without changing the final rows.
  • With LEFT JOIN and other outer joins, moving a condition between ON and WHERE can change the result significantly.
  • A right-table condition in ON can preserve unmatched left rows.
  • A right-table condition in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows and effectively turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER-style result.
practice: Step 1: Create the following sample tables and data.

customers
customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob

orders
order_id | customer_id | status
---------|-------------|----------
101      | 1           | PAID
102      | 1           | CANCELLED
103      | 2           | PAID
Step 2: Write an INNER JOIN using ON to connect customers and orders.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Step 3: Add a WHERE condition to return only PAID orders.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
Step 4: Rewrite the previous query by moving the PAID condition into ON. Compare the result.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID';
Step 5: Change the query to LEFT JOIN and put o.status = 'PAID' in the ON clause. Check whether Bob remains in the result.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'PAID';
Step 6: Move the same condition to WHERE and compare the result with Step 5.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
Step 7: Explain why Bob appears in Step 5 but disappears in Step 6. This is the most important exercise for this topic.
Step 8: Create an inventory example where every product must be preserved but only ACTIVE inventory records should match. Decide whether the status condition belongs in ON or WHERE.
Practice Goal: You should be able to decide whether a condition belongs in ON or WHERE, especially when using LEFT JOIN, and understand why moving a condition can change the result.

qna.q: Q1. What is the main purpose of ON?
qna.a: ON defines the matching condition between rows from the joined tables.

qna.q: Q2. What is the main purpose of WHERE?
qna.a: WHERE filters rows from the query result according to the required conditions.

qna.q: Q3. Are ON and WHERE interchangeable?
qna.a: No. With INNER JOIN, some conditions can often be moved between them without changing the result, but with OUTER JOINs such as LEFT JOIN, moving a condition can significantly change the result.

qna.q: Q4. Why is the difference especially important with LEFT JOIN?
qna.a: A LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched rows from the left table. A WHERE condition on a right-table column can remove those NULL-extended rows.

qna.q: Q5. What happens when a right-table condition is placed in ON during a LEFT JOIN?
qna.a: The condition controls which right-side rows are allowed to match, while unmatched left-side rows can still remain.

qna.q: Q6. What happens when a right-table condition is placed in WHERE during a LEFT JOIN?
qna.a: The WHERE condition filters the final rows. If the right-side value is NULL for an unmatched row, a condition such as status = 'PAID' will reject that row.

qna.q: Q7. Can ON contain more than the primary-key/foreign-key relationship?
qna.a: Yes. ON can contain additional conditions that determine which right-side rows should match.

qna.q: Q8. Which should I use for a condition like customer_id = customer_id?
qna.a: Use it in ON because it defines the relationship between the tables.

qna.q: Q9. Where should I normally put a final business filter such as price > 10000?
qna.a: Normally in WHERE when the intention is to filter the final result. However, with an OUTER JOIN, placement must be chosen carefully because moving the condition to ON can change which rows are preserved.

qna.q: Q10. What is the easiest rule to remember?
qna.a: Think: ON decides which rows MATCH; WHERE decides which rows STAY in the final result.

items.title: Understanding Duplicate Rows in Joins
explanation: What Are Duplicate Rows in Joins?
When you join two or more tables, the number of rows in the result can become larger than expected. This usually happens because one row from one table matches multiple rows from another table.
This is not necessarily a SQL error. It is usually the natural result of the relationship between the tables.
Definition: Duplicate rows in JOIN results occur when a row from one table matches multiple rows from another table, causing that row's information to appear multiple times in the result.
The Most Important Concept: JOIN Matches Rows
A JOIN does not automatically return one row per row from the first table. It returns rows based on the number of matching combinations between the joined tables.

Table A                    Table B

A1  ───────────────────→   B1
                         B2
                         B3

One A row matches 3 B rows

Result:
A1 + B1
A1 + B2
A1 + B3
Therefore, seeing the same value from the first table multiple times does not automatically mean SQL created an incorrect duplicate.
Simple Example
John has three orders. When customers are joined with orders, John appears three times because there are three matching order rows.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Result:

customer_id | name  | order_id
------------|-------|---------
1           | John  | 101
1           | John  | 102
1           | John  | 103
2           | Alice | 104
John is not actually duplicated as a customer record. Each result row represents a different customer-order relationship.
One-to-Many Relationship
This is one of the most common reasons for repeated rows.

Customer
   |
   | 1
   ↓
Orders
   |
   | many
   ↓
101, 102, 103
One customer can have many orders. Therefore, joining customers to orders naturally produces multiple result rows for that customer.
Many-to-Many Relationship
Many-to-many relationships can produce even larger row multiplication.

Student A
   ↓
Course 1
Course 2
Course 3

Student B
   ↓
Course 1
Course 2
A bridge table such as enrollments can connect students and courses. Each matching combination becomes a result row.
How Row Multiplication Happens
Suppose one customer has 3 orders and each order has 2 payment records.

1 Customer
    ↓
3 Orders
    ↓
2 Payments per Order
    ↓
6 joined combinations
The result can contain six rows for that customer because the JOIN combines matching records according to the relationships.
Duplicate Rows After Joining Two Tables
Consider an inventory example:
If you join only using part_no:

SELECT
    p.part_no,
    p.part_name,
    i.store_code,
    i.quantity
FROM parts p
JOIN inventory i
    ON p.part_no = i.part_no;
The part appears three times because the inventory table contains three matching rows.
Incorrect Join Condition Can Create Unexpected Multiplication
A particularly dangerous situation occurs when the JOIN condition is not specific enough.
Suppose inventory is actually identified by both part_no and store_code. Joining only on part_no may match multiple rows.

-- Potentially incomplete relationship
ON p.part_no = i.part_no
If the real relationship requires multiple columns, the JOIN may need:

ON p.part_no = i.part_no
AND p.store_code = i.store_code
Important: Before deciding that JOIN duplicates are a problem, identify the actual business key and relationship between the tables. A JOIN may be correct even when it produces repeated values.
Duplicate Values vs Duplicate Rows
These are not the same thing.

customer_id | name | order_id
------------|------|---------
1           | John | 101
1           | John | 102
1           | John | 103
The values customer_id = 1 and name = John repeat, but the complete rows are different because order_id is different.
A real duplicate row would look like:

customer_id | name | order_id
------------|------|---------
1           | John | 101
1           | John | 101
Here the complete result rows are identical.
How to Diagnose Unexpected Duplicates
Do not immediately use DISTINCT. First determine why the rows are multiplying.
Step 1: Check the base table.

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1;
Step 2: Check how many rows exist for the key.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Step 3: Check the JOIN condition.
ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
Ask whether one customer is expected to have multiple matching orders.
Step 4: Add tables one at a time.

customers
   ↓
customers + orders
   ↓
customers + orders + products
   ↓
customers + orders + products + payments
Check the row count after each JOIN. The JOIN where the row count unexpectedly increases is the first place to investigate.
Using COUNT to Find Duplicate Keys
You can identify keys that appear multiple times in a table.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS count_rows
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
This tells you which customers have multiple order records. That may be completely valid depending on the business rules.
Using DISTINCT
DISTINCT removes duplicate complete result rows.

SELECT DISTINCT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
This can return one row per unique customer in the selected columns.
Warning: DISTINCT should not be used simply to hide unexpected JOIN multiplication. First understand why the rows were multiplied. Otherwise, you may hide a data or query problem.
Why DISTINCT Can Be Dangerous
Suppose you have:

order_id | product_id | quantity
---------|------------|---------
101      | P100       | 5
101      | P100       | 7
If you use DISTINCT on selected columns that exclude quantity:

SELECT DISTINCT
    order_id,
    product_id
FROM ...;
the two rows may appear as one result row even though the underlying records are different.
JOIN Multiplication and Aggregates
This is especially important in Data Engineering because incorrect JOINs can produce incorrect totals.
Suppose:
If order 101 is joined to two payment rows and you then calculate an order amount using the joined result, the order amount can be repeated.

SELECT
    SUM(o.amount) AS total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p
    ON o.order_id = p.order_id;
Order 101's amount can appear twice in the joined result, so the SUM can become larger than the true order total.
Data Engineering Warning: A JOIN can change the grain of your data. Always determine the grain before performing SUM, COUNT, AVG, or other aggregations.
Understanding Grain
Grain means what one row represents.

orders
→ one row = one order

order_items
→ one row = one order item

payments
→ one row = one payment
If you join orders with order_items, the result is no longer necessarily one row per order. It can become one row per order item.

Before JOIN:
1 row = 1 order

After JOIN with order_items:
1 row = 1 order item

Therefore:
1 order with 4 items → 4 result rows
Pre-Aggregating Before a JOIN
Sometimes you need to aggregate a one-to-many table before joining it to another table.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    p.payment_count
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT
        order_id,
        COUNT(*) AS payment_count
    FROM payments
    GROUP BY order_id
) p
    ON o.order_id = p.order_id;
The payment table is first reduced to one row per order. Then it can be safely joined to the orders table at the order grain.
Data Engineering Example: Inventory
Suppose a report contains:

partmaster
→ one row per part

inventory
→ one row per part + store

stores
→ one row per store
If you join partmaster to inventory using only the part number, one part can legitimately appear multiple times because it exists in multiple stores.

SELECT
    p.part_no,
    i.store_code,
    i.quantity,
    s.store_name
FROM partmaster p
JOIN inventory i
    ON p.part_no = i.part_no
JOIN stores s
    ON i.store_code = s.store_code;
The correct result may contain several rows for the same part because the report grain is part + store, not simply part.
When Duplicates Are Actually a Problem

• The business requirement expects one row per key, but the query returns multiple rows.
  • The JOIN condition is incomplete.
  • A many-to-many relationship was not expected.
  • An aggregate is being calculated at the wrong grain.
  • Reference data contains unexpected duplicate keys.
  • A JOIN accidentally creates a Cartesian product.
When Repeated Rows Are Correct

• One customer has many orders.
  • One order has many order items.
  • One product exists in multiple stores.
  • One employee manages multiple employees.
  • One student is enrolled in multiple courses.
Practical Debugging Checklist

1. What does one row in each table represent?
  2. What is the primary key of each table?
  3. Is the JOIN one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many?
  4. Is the JOIN condition complete?
  5. Did the row count increase after a particular JOIN?
  6. Are duplicate keys present in either table?
  7. Did the JOIN change the grain?
  8. Will an aggregate now count or sum repeated rows?
  9. Can the one-to-many side be pre-aggregated before joining?
  10. Only after understanding the cause, decide whether DISTINCT or another technique is appropriate.
Quick Summary

• JOINs return matching row combinations, not necessarily one row per source-table row.
  • One-to-many relationships naturally produce repeated values.
  • Repeated values are not always duplicate rows.
  • Many-to-many relationships can multiply rows significantly.
  • An incomplete JOIN condition can create unexpected multiplication.
  • JOINs can change the grain of your data.
  • Incorrect JOIN multiplication can produce incorrect SUM and COUNT results.
  • Do not blindly use DISTINCT to hide duplicate rows.
  • For complex pipelines, check row counts and grain after every important JOIN.
practice: Step 1: Create the following customers and orders data.

customers
customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice

orders
order_id | customer_id | amount
---------|-------------|-------
101      | 1           | 1000
102      | 1           | 2000
103      | 1           | 3000
104      | 2           | 1500
Step 2: Join the tables and observe how many times John appears.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Step 3: Explain why John appears three times. Identify the grain of the result.
Step 4: Use GROUP BY to count how many orders each customer has.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY
    c.customer_id,
    c.name;
Step 5: Create an inventory table containing multiple stores for the same part. Join it with a parts table and identify why the part appears multiple times.
Step 6: Create a payments table where one order has multiple payment records. Join orders with payments and observe how the order amount is repeated.
Step 7: Calculate the total order amount after joining orders and payments. Check whether the result is correct or inflated because of row multiplication.
Step 8: Pre-aggregate the payments table to one row per order and then join it with orders. Compare the result with Step 7.

SELECT
    order_id,
    COUNT(*) AS payment_count
FROM payments
GROUP BY order_id;
Step 9: For a JOIN that unexpectedly returns duplicate-looking rows, do not use DISTINCT immediately. First check the row count and identify which JOIN causes the multiplication.

Practice Goal: You should be able to distinguish legitimate repeated rows from incorrect JOIN duplication, identify one-to-many and many-to-many row multiplication, understand grain, and prevent incorrect aggregations caused by JOINs.

qna.q: Q1. Why do rows repeat after a JOIN?
qna.a: Rows repeat when one row from one table matches multiple rows from the other table.

qna.q: Q2. Are repeated values always duplicate rows?
qna.a: No. A customer appearing multiple times can be correct if each result row represents a different order.

qna.q: Q3. What is the most common cause of repeated rows?
qna.a: A one-to-many relationship, where one row in one table matches multiple rows in another table.

qna.q: Q4. How can an incomplete JOIN condition create duplicates?
qna.a: If the real relationship requires multiple columns but the query joins using only part of the key, one row can match several rows unexpectedly.

qna.q: Q5. What is data grain?
qna.a: Grain describes what one row in a dataset represents, such as one order, one order item, or one part-store combination.

qna.q: Q6. Why can JOIN duplicates cause incorrect SUM results?
qna.a: If a row containing an amount is repeated by a one-to-many JOIN, SUM may add the same amount multiple times.

qna.q: Q7. Should DISTINCT always be used to remove duplicate rows?
qna.a: No. DISTINCT can hide the real cause of row multiplication and may remove legitimate differences from the result.

qna.q: Q8. How can you find which JOIN causes unexpected duplication?
qna.a: Add JOINs one at a time and compare the row count after each JOIN.

qna.q: Q9. How can pre-aggregation help with JOIN duplication?
qna.a: You can aggregate the many-side table to the required grain before joining it, reducing multiple matching rows to one row per key.

qna.q: Q10. What should you check before joining tables in a Data Engineering pipeline?
qna.a: Check each table's grain, primary key, foreign key, relationship cardinality, duplicate keys, JOIN condition, and the expected grain of the final result.

items.title: Understanding Missing Matches in Joins
explanation: What Are Missing Matches in JOINs?
A missing match occurs when a row from one table does not have a corresponding row in the table being joined.
This is especially important when working with LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN, because these JOINs can preserve rows even when a matching record does not exist.
Definition: A missing match means that a row in one table has no corresponding row in the other table according to the JOIN condition.
Simple Example
Suppose we have customers and orders:
John and Alice have orders, but Bob and David do not have matching rows in the orders table.
INNER JOIN and Missing Matches
An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match on both sides.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Result:

customer_id | name  | order_id
------------|-------|---------
1           | John  | 101
1           | John  | 103
2           | Alice | 102
Bob and David disappear because they have no matching orders.
Important: INNER JOIN does not show missing matches. It removes unmatched rows from the result.
LEFT JOIN and Missing Matches
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even when there is no matching row in the right table.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Result:

customer_id | name  | order_id
------------|-------|---------
1           | John  | 101
1           | John  | 103
2           | Alice | 102
3           | Bob   | NULL
4           | David | NULL
Bob and David are preserved, but the columns from orders contain NULL because no matching order exists.

customers                 orders

John  ─────────────────→  Order 101
John  ─────────────────→  Order 103
Alice ─────────────────→  Order 102
Bob   ────────────────X   No match
David ───────────────X    No match

LEFT JOIN keeps Bob and David.
Finding Missing Matches with LEFT JOIN
One of the most useful patterns in SQL is using LEFT JOIN followed by WHERE right_table.key IS NULL.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;
This returns customers who have no matching order.

customer_id | name
------------|------
3           | Bob
4           | David
Key Pattern: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right_table.key IS NULL is a common way to find records in the left table that have no matching record in the right table.
Why Does the Right Side Become NULL?
When a LEFT JOIN cannot find a matching row, SQL preserves the left-side row and fills the right-side columns with NULL.

Left row exists
      ↓
SQL searches for matching right row
      ↓
No match found
      ↓
Left row preserved
      ↓
Right-side columns = NULL
Finding Customers Who Have Orders
You can use the opposite condition to find customers that do have a match.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL;
However, if the goal is simply to return customers with at least one order, an INNER JOIN or EXISTS may be clearer depending on the query requirement.
RIGHT JOIN and Missing Matches
A RIGHT JOIN preserves every row from the right table.

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
If an order contains a customer ID that does not exist in the customers table, that order can still appear, while customer columns become NULL.

customers                 orders

John  ←────────────────  Order 101
Alice ←────────────────  Order 102
NULL  ←────────────────  Order 999

RIGHT JOIN preserves the right-side order.
FULL OUTER JOIN and Missing Matches
A FULL OUTER JOIN preserves rows from both tables, including rows that do not have matches.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
The result can contain:

• Rows that matched on both sides.
  • Customers without orders.
  • Orders without customers.

FULL OUTER JOIN

Matched:
Customer + Order

Left-only:
Customer + NULL

Right-only:
NULL + Order
Missing Matches Are Useful
Missing matches are not always errors. They can provide valuable information.

• Customers who have never placed an order.
  • Products that have no inventory.
  • Employees without assigned managers.
  • Orders with missing customer records.
  • Reference data that is missing from a source system.
  • Records that failed to map during an ETL process.
Data Engineering Example: Missing Reference Data
Suppose an ETL pipeline receives transactions containing product IDs and enriches them using a product master table.

transactions
--------------------------
transaction_id | product_id
--------------------------
1001           | P100
1002           | P200
1003           | P999

product_master
--------------------------
product_id | product_name
--------------------------
P100       | Laptop
P200       | Keyboard
Product P999 does not exist in the product master.

SELECT
    t.transaction_id,
    t.product_id,
    p.product_name
FROM transactions t
LEFT JOIN product_master p
    ON t.product_id = p.product_id;
The result contains:

transaction_id | product_id | product_name
---------------|------------|-------------
1001           | P100       | Laptop
1002           | P200       | Keyboard
1003           | P999       | NULL
This can identify a data-quality problem: a transaction references a product that does not exist in the master data.
Finding Orphan Records
An orphan record is a record that refers to another record that does not exist.
Definition: An orphan record is a row containing a reference to a related entity that cannot be found in the referenced table.
For example, an order whose customer_id does not exist in the customer master is an orphan order.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
This is a very useful data-quality query because it finds orders without a valid customer.
Missing Matches in ETL Pipelines

Source Transactions
        ↓
    JOIN Master Data
        ↓
   Match Found?
      /      \
    YES       NO
     ↓         ↓
 Enriched    Data Quality
   Data       Exception
               ↓
          Error / Reject
          / Quarantine
A production pipeline may separate unmatched records instead of silently dropping them.
Missing Matches and NULL
Do not confuse a missing match with a NULL value that already exists in the source data.
For example, a customer may exist but have a NULL phone number:

customer_id | name  | phone
------------|-------|------
1           | John  | NULL
This does not mean the customer is missing. It means the customer exists but the phone value is unknown or absent.
By contrast:

customer_id | name  | order_id
------------|-------|---------
3           | Bob   | NULL
Here the NULL order information can indicate that the customer has no matching order.
Important: NULL does not always mean missing record. It can mean an unknown, unavailable, or not-applicable value. The meaning depends on the column and query context.
Missing Matches and JOIN Conditions
A row can appear unmatched because the JOIN condition is incorrect or incomplete, not because the related data is truly missing.
For example, suppose a relationship requires both part_no and store_code.

ON a.part_no = b.part_no
AND a.store_code = b.store_code
If you accidentally join using only:
ON a.part_no = b.part_no
you may get incorrect matches or unexpected multiple rows. Therefore, always verify the actual business key before diagnosing a missing match.
Common Reasons for Missing Matches

• The related record genuinely does not exist.
  • Different values are used to represent the same entity.
  • Leading or trailing spaces exist in text keys.
  • Different data types or formats are used.
  • Case differences matter in the database's comparison rules.
  • The JOIN condition is incomplete.
  • The wrong column was used for the JOIN.
  • Source data is incomplete or delayed.
  • Reference/master data has not yet been loaded.
Checking for Formatting Problems
Sometimes values look identical but are actually different.

Source value:   'P100 '
Master value:   'P100'
Depending on the database and data type, whitespace or formatting differences can prevent a match.
For troubleshooting, you may inspect values using functions such as TRIM(), but do not blindly apply functions to JOIN columns in production because they can affect index usage and performance.
Finding Missing Matches with NOT EXISTS
Another common pattern for finding unmatched records is NOT EXISTS.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
This finds customers for whom no matching order exists.
Both LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS are useful patterns. Which one is preferable can depend on the query, database, and business requirement.
Common Mistakes

• Using INNER JOIN when unmatched records need to be identified.
  • Filtering a right-side column in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN and unintentionally removing missing matches.
  • Assuming every NULL means the related record is missing.
  • Ignoring whitespace, formatting, or key-quality problems.
  • Assuming a missing match is always a data problem without checking the JOIN condition.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide a problem instead of understanding the relationship.
Quick Summary

• INNER JOIN removes unmatched rows.
  • LEFT JOIN preserves all rows from the left table and shows NULL for missing right-side matches.
  • RIGHT JOIN preserves all rows from the right table.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides.
  • LEFT JOIN + WHERE right_key IS NULL is a common anti-join pattern for finding missing matches.
  • Missing matches can identify data-quality problems and orphan records.
  • Always verify the JOIN condition before concluding that data is missing.
  • In Data Engineering, unmatched records are often handled through validation, rejection, quarantine, or exception reporting.
practice: Step 1: Create the following customers and orders data.

customers
customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
4           | David

orders
order_id | customer_id
---------|------------
101      | 1
102      | 2
103      | 1
104      | 99
Step 2: Use INNER JOIN and observe which customers are missing from the result.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Step 3: Use LEFT JOIN to display every customer, including customers without orders.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Step 4: Find customers who have no orders.

SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;
Step 5: Find orders that do not have a matching customer.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
Step 6: Rewrite Step 5 using NOT EXISTS.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id
FROM orders o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM customers c
    WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id
);
Step 7: Create a product master and transaction table. Add a transaction containing a product ID that does not exist in the master. Use LEFT JOIN to identify the unmatched transaction.
Step 8: Investigate an unmatched record by checking whether the JOIN key contains whitespace, different formatting, a different data type, or an incorrect value.
Step 9: Think like a Data Engineer: decide what your pipeline should do with unmatched records. Should they be rejected, quarantined, logged, or allowed through with NULL reference data?

Practice Goal: You should be able to identify missing relationships using LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, and NOT EXISTS, distinguish missing records from NULL values, and recognize unmatched data as an important Data Quality problem in Data Engineering.

qna.q: Q1. What is a missing match in a JOIN?
qna.a: It is a row from one table that has no corresponding row in the other table according to the JOIN condition.

qna.q: Q2. What happens to missing matches in an INNER JOIN?
qna.a: They are excluded from the result.

qna.q: Q3. What happens to missing matches in a LEFT JOIN?
qna.a: Rows from the left table are preserved, while columns from the right table become NULL when no match exists.

qna.q: Q4. How do you find rows in the left table that have no match in the right table?
qna.a: Use a LEFT JOIN and filter for NULL in a suitable right-table key column, for example WHERE right_table.key IS NULL.

qna.q: Q5. What is an orphan record?
qna.a: An orphan record is a row that references a related entity that does not exist in the referenced table.

qna.q: Q6. Can NULL always be interpreted as a missing record?
qna.a: No. NULL can represent an unknown, unavailable, or not-applicable value. Its meaning depends on the column and query context.

qna.q: Q7. Why might a row fail to match even when the values appear similar?
qna.a: Differences in whitespace, formatting, case behavior, data types, incorrect values, or an incomplete JOIN condition can prevent a match.

qna.q: Q8. How can missing matches be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They can identify data-quality problems such as missing reference data, invalid foreign keys, orphan records, or failed enrichment during an ETL pipeline.

qna.q: Q9. Can NOT EXISTS be used to find missing matches?
qna.a: Yes. NOT EXISTS is a common way to return rows for which no corresponding record exists in another table.

qna.q: Q10. What should you check before deciding that data is genuinely missing?
qna.a: Verify the JOIN condition, business key, data type, formatting, whitespace, source completeness, and whether the related record has already been loaded.

items.title: `UNION`
explanation: What is `UNION`?
UNION is a SQL set operation used to combine the result of two or more SELECT queries into a single result.
Unlike a JOIN, which combines columns from related tables, UNION combines the rows returned by separate queries.
Definition: UNION combines the results of multiple compatible SELECT statements and removes duplicate rows from the final result.
UNION vs JOIN

JOIN

Table A ───── JOIN ───── Table B
              ↓
       More columns / enriched rows

UNION

Query A ───── UNION ───── Query B
              ↓
       More rows / combined results
A simple way to remember it:
Remember: JOIN usually adds columns by combining related rows. UNION usually adds rows by stacking compatible result sets.
Basic Syntax

SELECT column1, column2
FROM table1

UNION

SELECT column1, column2
FROM table2;
Both SELECT statements must return compatible result structures.
Simple Example
Suppose two tables contain customers from different regions:

customers_india
-------------------------
customer_id | name
-------------------------
1           | John
2           | Alice

customers_usa
-------------------------
customer_id | name
-------------------------
3           | Bob
4           | David
We can combine them using UNION:

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa;
Result:

customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
4           | David
The result contains rows from both queries.
UNION Removes Duplicate Rows
The key characteristic of UNION is that it removes duplicate rows from the combined result.

SELECT name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT name
FROM customers_usa;
If both result sets contain:

John
Alice
the final UNION result contains each identical result row only once.
UNION Requires Compatible SELECT Statements
The SELECT statements used with UNION must have the same number of columns.
Valid:

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa;
Invalid:

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name, city
FROM customers_usa;
The first query returns two columns while the second returns three columns, so they cannot be combined using UNION.
Rule: Every SELECT participating in a UNION must return the same number of columns, in the same positional order, with compatible data types.
Column Names in UNION Results
The column names of the final result generally come from the first SELECT statement.

SELECT
    customer_id AS id,
    name AS customer_name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name
FROM customers_usa;
The final result uses the column names from the first SELECT:

id | customer_name
---|--------------
Therefore, it is good practice to make the first SELECT clearly define the desired output column names.
Column Position Matters
UNION matches columns by their position, not by column name.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name
FROM customers_usa;
The first column is combined with the first column, and the second column with the second column.
Important: UNION does not match columns by their names. It combines them according to their position in each SELECT list.
Compatible Data Types
The corresponding columns should contain compatible data types.
For example, this is generally reasonable:

SELECT customer_id
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id
FROM customers_usa;
Both positions represent customer IDs.
But mixing unrelated or incompatible data types can result in an error or implicit conversion depending on the database system.
UNION with Different Source Tables
The source tables do not have to have the same table name or structure internally. Only the SELECT results need to be compatible.

SELECT
    employee_id,
    employee_name
FROM employees

UNION

SELECT
    contractor_id,
    contractor_name
FROM contractors;
This can create a combined list of people from two different sources.
UNION with Different Column Names
The source columns can have different names as long as the selected values are compatible.

SELECT
    employee_id,
    employee_name
FROM employees

UNION

SELECT
    contractor_id,
    contractor_name
FROM contractors;
The result column names will normally come from the first SELECT.
Adding a Source Column
A useful Data Engineering technique is adding a constant to identify where each row came from.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'INDIA' AS source
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'USA' AS source
FROM customers_usa;
Result:

customer_id | name  | source
------------|-------|-------
1           | John  | INDIA
2           | Alice | INDIA
3           | Bob   | USA
4           | David | USA
This is especially useful when combining data from multiple systems or regions.
UNION with WHERE
Each SELECT can have its own filtering conditions.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
Each source is filtered before its results are combined.
UNION with ORDER BY
If you want to sort the final combined result, place the ORDER BY after the UNION query.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa

ORDER BY name;
This sorts the final combined result.

Important: An ORDER BY placed at the end normally controls the final UNION result. Database-specific rules may apply when ordering by expressions or columns not directly exposed by the combined result.
UNION with Multiple Queries
You can combine more than two SELECT statements.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_uk;
The result combines all three result sets and removes duplicate result rows.
UNION in Data Engineering
UNION is useful when data with the same logical structure comes from multiple sources.

Source A
  ↓
SELECT / Transform
  ↓
      ┐
      │
Source B → SELECT / Transform ──→ UNION → Combined Dataset
      │
      ┘
Source C
  ↓
SELECT / Transform
Common examples include:

• Combining regional datasets.
  • Combining historical and current datasets.
  • Combining records from multiple source systems.
  • Combining employee and contractor records.
  • Combining partitioned source tables.
  • Creating a unified staging dataset before transformation.
Example: Combining Monthly Data
Suppose separate tables contain monthly sales:

sales_january
sales_february
sales_march
If all tables have the same logical structure:

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_january

UNION

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_february

UNION

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_march;
The query creates one combined result containing data from all three months.
UNION and Duplicate Business Records
UNION removes duplicate result rows, but that does not necessarily mean it removes duplicate business records correctly.
For example:

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM source_a

UNION

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM source_b;
If two sources contain the same order ID but different amounts, both rows may remain because the complete rows are different.
Important: UNION removes duplicate result rows, not duplicate business entities based on a key you have in mind.
UNION vs UNION ALL
The major difference is duplicate handling.

OperationCombines RowsRemoves Duplicate Result RowsTypical Use
UNIONYesYesWhen duplicate result rows should be removed
UNION ALLYesNoWhen all rows should be retained
UNION ALL is covered separately in the next topic because duplicate handling and performance are important considerations in Data Engineering.
UNION vs JOIN

FeatureUNIONJOIN
Main PurposeCombine result sets verticallyCombine related rows horizontally
Result ShapeUsually more rowsUsually more columns
Relationship RequiredNo table relationship requiredUsually requires a matching condition
Column RequirementSame number of compatible columnsCan select different columns from each table
Common Mistakes

• Using UNION when a JOIN is actually required.
  • Returning different numbers of columns in the SELECT statements.
  • Returning incompatible data types in corresponding positions.
  • Assuming UNION matches columns by name instead of position.
  • Forgetting that UNION removes duplicate result rows.
  • Using UNION when all source rows should be preserved.
  • Assuming UNION removes duplicate business entities based on a particular ID.
  • Putting the final ORDER BY in the wrong place.
Quick Summary

• UNION combines the results of multiple SELECT statements.
  • It stacks result rows vertically.
  • Each SELECT must return the same number of compatible columns.
  • Corresponding columns are matched by position.
  • The final result removes duplicate rows.
  • The final column names normally come from the first SELECT.
  • A source column can be added to identify where each row came from.
  • UNION is useful for combining similar datasets from multiple sources.
  • Use UNION when duplicate result rows should be removed; use UNION ALL when all rows should be retained.
practice: Step 1: Create two tables containing customers from two different regions with the same logical structure.

customers_india
customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice

customers_usa
customer_id | name
------------|------
3           | Bob
4           | David
Step 2: Use UNION to combine both customer lists.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa;
Step 3: Add the same customer to both tables and observe how UNION handles the duplicate result row.
Step 4: Add a constant source column so that each row shows which region it came from.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'INDIA' AS source
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'USA' AS source
FROM customers_usa;
Step 5: Filter each source to include only ACTIVE customers before combining them.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
Step 6: Create three monthly sales tables with the same structure and combine January, February, and March using UNION.
Step 7: Add an extra column to only one SELECT and observe the error. Then correct the query so that all SELECT statements return the same number of columns.
Step 8: Sort the final combined result by customer name using ORDER BY.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa

ORDER BY name;

Step 9: Before using UNION in a Data Engineering pipeline, verify that the SELECT statements represent the same logical grain. For example, do not combine one result containing one row per order with another containing one row per order item without intentionally transforming them first.

Practice Goal: You should be able to combine compatible result sets using UNION, understand its duplicate-removal behavior, correctly align columns, and recognize when UNION is more appropriate than JOIN.

qna.q: Q1. What is UNION in SQL?
qna.a: UNION combines the results of two or more SELECT queries into a single result and removes duplicate result rows.

qna.q: Q2. Does UNION add rows or columns?
qna.a: UNION combines rows from multiple result sets. It is commonly thought of as stacking compatible results vertically.

qna.q: Q3. What requirement must SELECT statements satisfy when using UNION?
qna.a: They must return the same number of columns, with compatible data types in corresponding positions.

qna.q: Q4. Does UNION match columns by name?
qna.a: No. Corresponding columns are combined by their position in the SELECT lists.

qna.q: Q5. Does UNION remove duplicate rows?
qna.a: Yes. UNION removes duplicate complete result rows.

qna.q: Q6. Does UNION remove duplicate business records based on an ID?
qna.a: No. It removes duplicate result rows. If rows have different values in any selected column, both rows can remain even when they have the same business ID.

qna.q: Q7. Can UNION combine data from tables with different column names?
qna.a: Yes. The source column names can differ as long as the selected result columns are compatible and positioned correctly.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between UNION and JOIN?
qna.a: UNION combines compatible result sets by stacking rows, while JOIN combines related rows from tables and can bring columns from those tables into the result.

qna.q: Q9. Can a UNION contain more than two SELECT statements?
qna.a: Yes. Multiple SELECT statements can be connected using UNION.

qna.q: Q10. Why is UNION useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can combine similarly structured data from different regions, source systems, time periods, or staging datasets into one logical result.

items.title: `UNION ALL`
explanation: What is `UNION ALL`?
UNION ALL is a SQL set operation used to combine the results of two or more SELECT statements into one result set while keeping all rows, including duplicate rows.
It is similar to UNION, but the most important difference is that UNION ALL does not remove duplicates.
Definition: UNION ALL combines compatible SELECT result sets and preserves every row returned by every SELECT statement.
UNION vs UNION ALL

UNION

Query A ──┐
          ├── Combine → Remove duplicate result rows
Query B ──┘

UNION ALL

Query A ──┐
          ├── Combine → Keep every row
Query B ──┘

FeatureUNIONUNION ALL
Combines result setsYesYes
Keeps duplicate rowsNoYes
Duplicate removalYesNo
Typical processingRequires duplicate eliminationCan return rows without duplicate elimination
Common Data Engineering useWhen duplicate result rows should be removedWhen every source row should be preserved
Basic Syntax

SELECT column1, column2
FROM table1

UNION ALL

SELECT column1, column2
FROM table2;
As with UNION, the SELECT statements must return the same number of compatible columns in corresponding positions.
Simple Example
Suppose two tables contain customer records:

customers_india
-------------------------
customer_id | name
-------------------------
1           | John
2           | Alice

customers_usa
-------------------------
customer_id | name
-------------------------
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
Using UNION ALL:

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION ALL

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa;
Result:

customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
The Alice row appears twice because UNION ALL preserves every row.
Compare with UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_india

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_usa;
The duplicate Alice result row is removed:

customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
Remember: UNION means combine and remove duplicate result rows. UNION ALL means combine and keep every result row.
Why Would We Want Duplicate Rows?
A duplicate-looking row is not necessarily an unwanted duplicate. It may represent two legitimate records from different source systems, dates, transactions, or partitions.
For example, suppose two source systems each contain an order:

source_a
order_id | amount
---------|-------
1001     | 500

source_b
order_id | amount
---------|-------
1001     | 500
If these are two legitimate source records, UNION ALL preserves both rows.
UNION ALL in Data Engineering
UNION ALL is especially important in Data Engineering because pipelines often need to append data without silently removing records.

Source A
   ↓
Transform
   ↓
   ┐
   │
   ├── UNION ALL → Combined Dataset
   │
   ┘
Source B
   ↓
Transform
Typical use cases include:

• Appending daily files.
  • Combining monthly partitions.
  • Combining regional source systems.
  • Appending incremental batches.
  • Combining historical and newly arrived records.
  • Building staging datasets from multiple sources.
Example: Combining Daily Data
Imagine separate tables for daily sales:

sales_2026_10_01
sales_2026_10_02
sales_2026_10_03
If every table contains the same logical type of rows:

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_2026_10_01

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_2026_10_02

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM sales_2026_10_03;
This appends all rows into one result.
Why UNION ALL Is Often Preferred for Appending Data
If the source data is already known to contain valid independent records, removing duplicates can be unnecessary or even incorrect.
For example:

January sales → 100,000 rows
February sales → 120,000 rows
March sales → 110,000 rows

UNION ALL

Expected combined rows = 330,000
Using UNION would ask the database to eliminate identical result rows even though those rows may represent legitimate transactions.
Data Engineering Rule: When appending independent datasets and every source row should be retained, UNION ALL is usually the appropriate operation.
UNION ALL Does Not Mean the Data Is Wrong
Suppose two rows are identical:

order_id | amount
---------|-------
1001     | 500
1001     | 500
UNION ALL keeps both rows because it does not determine whether they represent duplicate business events or two legitimate events.
The responsibility for deciding whether these are valid records belongs to the data model and business rules.
UNION ALL and Business Keys
A business key can help determine whether repeated records represent duplicates.
If order_id is supposed to be globally unique, two identical order IDs may require investigation. But UNION ALL itself should not automatically delete one.
UNION ALL with a Source Identifier
A useful technique is adding a source column before combining datasets.

SELECT
    order_id,
    amount,
    'SYSTEM_A' AS source_system
FROM orders_a

UNION ALL

SELECT
    order_id,
    amount,
    'SYSTEM_B' AS source_system
FROM orders_b;
Now, if the same order ID appears twice, you can determine where each record came from.

order_id | amount | source_system
---------|--------|--------------
1001     | 500    | SYSTEM_A
1001     | 500    | SYSTEM_B
UNION ALL with Different Filters
Each SELECT can have its own filtering conditions.

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders_a
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders_b
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED';
Each source is filtered first, and the resulting rows are then appended.
UNION ALL with ORDER BY
To sort the final combined result, place ORDER BY after the complete UNION ALL operation.

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders_a

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders_b

ORDER BY amount DESC;
This sorts the final combined result by amount.
UNION ALL and Aggregation
You can aggregate after combining datasets.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, amount
    FROM orders_a

    UNION ALL

    SELECT customer_id, amount
    FROM orders_b
) combined_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
The inner UNION ALL creates one combined dataset, and the outer query calculates the total for each customer.
Important: Because UNION ALL preserves every row, any duplicate or repeated source records will also participate in later COUNT, SUM, AVG, and other aggregations.
UNION ALL and Data Quality
UNION ALL preserves source data, so duplicate detection can be performed as a separate data-quality step.

SELECT
    order_id,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM (
    SELECT order_id FROM orders_a
    UNION ALL
    SELECT order_id FROM orders_b
) combined
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
This can help identify order IDs appearing multiple times across the combined sources.
UNION ALL vs JOIN

FeatureUNION ALLJOIN
Main PurposeAppend result setsCombine related rows
Result ShapeUsually more rowsOften more columns
Relationship RequiredNoUsually yes
Duplicate HandlingKeeps all rowsDepends on relationships
UNION ALL vs UNION vs JOIN

UNION
A + B → rows combined → duplicate result rows removed

UNION ALL
A + B → rows combined → every row retained

JOIN
A + B → related rows matched → columns combined
Common Mistakes

• Using UNION ALL when duplicate result rows should actually be removed.
  • Assuming UNION ALL automatically detects duplicate business records.
  • Using UNION ALL to combine datasets with different logical grains.
  • Forgetting that repeated rows will affect later aggregations.
  • Using DISTINCT later as a blind fix instead of understanding the source duplication.
  • Forgetting to add a source column when tracing records from multiple systems.
Quick Summary

• UNION ALL combines multiple SELECT result sets.
  • It preserves every row.
  • It does not remove duplicate result rows.
  • SELECT statements must return the same number of compatible columns.
  • Columns are combined by position.
  • It is commonly useful for appending batches, partitions, regions, or source-system data.
  • Repeated records remain and can affect later aggregations.
  • Use a separate data-quality step if duplicate business records need to be detected.
  • For Data Engineering append operations, UNION ALL is often the natural choice when every source row must be preserved.
practice: Step 1: Create two tables containing customer records from different source systems.

customers_a
customer_id | name
------------|------
1           | John
2           | Alice

customers_b
customer_id | name
------------|------
2           | Alice
3           | Bob
Step 2: Use UNION ALL to combine both tables and observe the duplicate Alice row.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_a

UNION ALL

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_b;
Step 3: Run the same query using UNION and compare the number of rows.

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_a

UNION

SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers_b;
Step 4: Add a source-system column to determine where each row originated.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'SOURCE_A' AS source_system
FROM customers_a

UNION ALL

SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    'SOURCE_B' AS source_system
FROM customers_b;
Step 5: Create separate January, February, and March sales tables and combine them using UNION ALL.
Step 6: Count the total number of rows after combining the monthly datasets.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows
FROM (
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_january
    UNION ALL
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_february
    UNION ALL
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_march
) combined;
Step 7: Find IDs that appear more than once after combining the sources.

SELECT
    order_id,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM (
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_january
    UNION ALL
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_february
    UNION ALL
    SELECT order_id FROM sales_march
) combined
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Step 8: Build a Data Engineering example where two source systems contain the same logical order. Keep both records with UNION ALL first, then create a separate validation query to identify duplicate order IDs.
Step 9: Explain why UNION ALL is usually more appropriate than UNION when appending independent daily or monthly source data where every source row must be retained.

Practice Goal: You should be able to use UNION ALL to append compatible datasets, understand why duplicate rows are preserved, track source systems, and detect duplicate business keys separately from the append operation.

qna.q: Q1. What is UNION ALL?
qna.a: UNION ALL combines the results of two or more compatible SELECT statements and keeps every row, including duplicate result rows.

qna.q: Q2. What is the main difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
qna.a: UNION removes duplicate result rows, while UNION ALL preserves all rows.

qna.q: Q3. Does UNION ALL remove duplicate rows?
qna.a: No. UNION ALL does not perform duplicate elimination.

qna.q: Q4. Why is UNION ALL useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It is useful for appending independent datasets such as daily batches, monthly partitions, regional data, or records from multiple source systems while preserving every source row.

qna.q: Q5. Does UNION ALL determine whether two rows are duplicate business records?
qna.a: No. UNION ALL simply preserves rows. Business duplicate detection should be handled separately using keys, business rules, or data-quality logic.

qna.q: Q6. Can UNION ALL affect aggregate results?
qna.a: Yes. Because UNION ALL preserves every row, repeated records can affect COUNT, SUM, AVG, and other aggregations.
