Unlike UPDATE, which changes data inside rows, ALTER TABLE changes the table definition itself.
Definition: ALTER TABLE modifies the structure of an existing table by adding, removing, or changing supported columns and constraints.
Why Do We Need `ALTER TABLE`?
Suppose a table was created with three columns:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Later, you realize that the table also needs a department column. You do not need to delete and recreate the table. You can modify its structure using ALTER TABLE.

Existing Table
      │
      │ ALTER TABLE
      ↓
Modified Table Structure
      │
      ├── Existing columns
      ├── New columns
      └── Modified constraints
Basic Syntax

ALTER TABLE table_name
alteration;
The exact alteration syntax depends on the database system.
1. Add a Column
One of the most common uses of ALTER TABLE is adding a new column.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD COLUMN department VARCHAR(50);
The table now contains the additional department column.

Before:
employee_id | employee_name | salary

After ADD COLUMN:
employee_id | employee_name | salary | department
2. Add Multiple Columns
Some database systems support adding multiple columns in one statement.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD COLUMN department VARCHAR(50),
ADD COLUMN joining_date DATE;
Exact multi-column syntax can vary by database system.
3. Add a Column with a Default Value
You can define a default value when adding a column, depending on the database system.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Active';

The default can be used for future INSERT operations when the column is omitted. How existing rows are populated when adding a column with a default can depend on the database implementation and version.
4. Drop a Column
You can remove an existing column using DROP COLUMN.

ALTER TABLE employees
DROP COLUMN department;

Warning: Dropping a column removes that column from the table definition and can make its stored data inaccessible through that column. Always verify dependencies and data requirements before doing this in production.
5. Rename a Column
Many database systems support renaming a column with RENAME COLUMN.

ALTER TABLE employees
RENAME COLUMN employee_name TO full_name;
The column name changes from employee_name to full_name.
Database Note: Column-renaming syntax varies between database systems. Always use the syntax supported by your database.
6. Rename a Table
Some databases support renaming a table with RENAME TO.

ALTER TABLE employees
RENAME TO company_employees;
The table name changes from employees to company_employees.
7. Change a Column Data Type
Some database systems allow you to change the data type of an existing column.

ALTER TABLE employees
ALTER COLUMN salary TYPE DECIMAL(12, 2);
The exact syntax is database-specific. For example, PostgreSQL uses the shown ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE syntax, while other databases use different forms.
Important: Changing a data type can fail if existing values cannot be converted safely. It can also affect applications, queries and downstream pipelines.
8. Add a Primary Key
A primary key constraint can be added to an existing table when the existing data satisfies the required rules.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT pk_employees
PRIMARY KEY (employee_id);
The database will normally reject the operation if existing values violate primary-key requirements, such as duplicate or NULL values.
9. Add a Foreign Key
A foreign key can also be added after tables already exist.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);

customers
──────────────
customer_id PK
      │
      │ referenced by
      ↓
orders
──────────────
customer_id FK
The existing data must satisfy the foreign key relationship for the constraint to be added successfully.
10. Add a UNIQUE Constraint

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT uq_employees_email
UNIQUE (email);
This adds a uniqueness constraint to the email column.
11. Add a CHECK Constraint

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_employee_salary
CHECK (salary >= 0);
This requires the salary values to satisfy the specified condition according to the database's constraint rules.
12. Drop a Constraint
Named constraints can often be removed with DROP CONSTRAINT.

ALTER TABLE employees
DROP CONSTRAINT chk_employee_salary;
Constraint-removal syntax and behavior can vary by database system.
13. `ALTER TABLE` vs `UPDATE`

CommandChangesExample
ALTER TABLETable structureAdd a column
UPDATEExisting row valuesChange salary

ALTER TABLE
     ↓
Changes structure
     ↓
Columns / Constraints / Table definition

UPDATE
     ↓
Changes data
     ↓
Values inside existing rows
14. `ALTER TABLE` vs `CREATE TABLE`

CommandPurpose
CREATE TABLECreates a new table
ALTER TABLEChanges an existing table
15. Data Engineering Example: Schema Evolution
Data Engineering systems often need to handle schema evolution. For example, a source system may start sending a new field that was not present in the original target table.

Original Source Schema
id | name | amount
       ↓
New Source Version
id | name | amount | currency
       ↓
Target table must evolve
       ↓
ALTER TABLE
       ↓
id | name | amount | currency
For example:

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD COLUMN currency VARCHAR(10);
This is a simple example of schema evolution. In production, the change should also be coordinated with ingestion jobs, transformations, tests and downstream consumers.
16. Data Engineering Example: Adding a Pipeline Column
Suppose a staging table originally contains:

CREATE TABLE staging_orders (
    order_id INT,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
Later, the pipeline needs to record when the data was loaded.

ALTER TABLE staging_orders
ADD COLUMN load_timestamp TIMESTAMP;
The new column can then be populated by the ingestion or transformation process according to the pipeline design.
17. Adding a Column to a Production Table
Adding a column may appear simple, but production systems require more consideration.

CheckWhy?
Existing dataDetermine how old rows should behave
ApplicationsQueries may depend on the existing schema
ETL pipelinesTransformations may need modification
BI reportsReports may depend on table structure
PerformanceLarge tables can make schema changes expensive
DeploymentCoordinate schema and application changes
18. Why Schema Changes Matter in Data Engineering
A schema change can affect an entire data pipeline.

Source
  ↓
Ingestion
  ↓
Staging
  ↓
Transformation
  ↓
Warehouse
  ↓
BI / Reports

Schema change at one layer
          ↓
Potential impact on downstream layers
Data Engineering Tip: Treat schema changes as pipeline changes, not just database changes. Check upstream producers and downstream consumers before changing a shared table.
19. Common Mistakes

• Dropping a column without checking dependencies.
  • Changing a data type without checking whether existing values can be converted.
  • Adding a NOT NULL or key constraint when existing data violates it.
  • Renaming a column without updating downstream queries and pipelines.
  • Assuming ALTER TABLE syntax is identical across all databases.
  • Making production schema changes without testing them first.
  • Ignoring BI reports, ETL jobs, APIs or applications that depend on the table.
  • Adding a new column without defining how existing rows should be populated or interpreted.
Quick Summary

OperationPurpose
ADD COLUMNAdd a new column
DROP COLUMNRemove a column
RENAME COLUMNRename a column where supported
RENAME TORename a table where supported
Change data typeModify a column's type where supported
ADD CONSTRAINTAdd a key or validation constraint
DROP CONSTRAINTRemove a named constraint where supported
Data EngineeringImportant for schema evolution and pipeline maintenance
practice: Hands-On Practice: ALTER TABLE
Step 1: Create a basic employees table.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Step 2: Add a department column.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD COLUMN department VARCHAR(50);
Step 3: Verify the table structure using your database's table-description or information-schema tools.

SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'employees';
Step 4: Insert sample records using the new column.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, salary, department)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul', 35000, 'IT'),
    (102, 'Priya', 40000, 'HR'),
    (103, 'Arun', 45000, 'Finance');
Step 5: Add a new column to record the employee's joining date.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD COLUMN joining_date DATE;
Step 6: Add a salary validation constraint if your database supports the shown syntax.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_employee_salary
CHECK (salary >= 0);
Step 7: Create a customer table and an orders table.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
Step 8: Add a foreign key relationship between orders and customers.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
Step 9: Practice Data Engineering schema evolution by adding a load timestamp to a staging table.

CREATE TABLE staging_orders (
    order_id INT,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);

ALTER TABLE staging_orders
ADD COLUMN load_timestamp TIMESTAMP;
Step 10: Practice dropping a column only after verifying that it is no longer required.

ALTER TABLE employees
DROP COLUMN joining_date;
Step 11: If your database supports column renaming with the shown syntax, rename department to department_name.

ALTER TABLE employees
RENAME COLUMN department TO department_name;
Step 12: Document which downstream systems would need to be checked if the department column were renamed in a real Data Engineering pipeline.

Practice Goal: You should be able to add and remove columns, understand constraint changes, modify an existing table structure, and recognize why schema changes must be coordinated with Data Engineering pipelines and downstream consumers.

qna.q: Q1. What is `ALTER TABLE`?
qna.a: `ALTER TABLE` is a DDL command used to modify the structure of an existing table.

qna.q: Q2. What is the difference between ALTER TABLE and UPDATE?
qna.a: `ALTER TABLE` changes the table structure, while `UPDATE` changes values inside existing rows.

qna.q: Q3. How do you add a column?
qna.a: A common syntax is `ALTER TABLE table_name ADD COLUMN column_name data_type;`.

qna.q: Q4. How do you remove a column?
qna.a: Where supported, use `ALTER TABLE table_name DROP COLUMN column_name;`.

qna.q: Q5. Can ALTER TABLE rename a column?
qna.a: Yes. Many database systems support column renaming, but the exact syntax differs by database.

qna.q: Q6. Can ALTER TABLE rename a table?
qna.a: Yes. Many database systems support table renaming through ALTER TABLE, although the exact syntax varies.

qna.q: Q7. Can ALTER TABLE change a column's data type?
qna.a: Many database systems support changing column data types, but the syntax differs and existing values must be compatible with the new type.

qna.q: Q8. Can ALTER TABLE add constraints?
qna.a: Yes. It can be used to add constraints such as PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE and CHECK where supported.

qna.q: Q9. Why can adding a constraint fail?
qna.a: It can fail when existing data violates the constraint. For example, duplicate values can prevent a unique constraint from being added.

qna.q: Q10. Why is DROP COLUMN dangerous?
qna.a: Dropping a column can remove access to its stored data and can break queries, applications, reports and pipelines that depend on it.

qna.q: Q11. What is schema evolution?
qna.a: Schema evolution is the process of changing a data structure over time as new fields, requirements or data definitions are introduced.

qna.q: Q12. How is ALTER TABLE useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It is useful for controlled schema evolution, such as adding new fields required by changing source systems or pipeline requirements.

qna.q: Q13. Is ALTER TABLE syntax the same for every database?
qna.a: No. The general concept is similar, but syntax and supported operations vary between PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and other platforms.

qna.q: Q14. What should you check before changing a production table?
qna.a: Check existing data, constraints, ETL pipelines, applications, BI reports, downstream consumers, performance impact and the organization's deployment or change-management process.

qna.q: Q15. Why is ALTER TABLE important for Data Engineers?
qna.a: Data pipelines evolve over time. Data Engineers need to understand how schema changes affect ingestion, transformation, storage and downstream consumers.

qna.q: Q16. What is the difference between CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE?
qna.a: `CREATE TABLE` creates a new table, while `ALTER TABLE` changes an existing table's structure.

items.title: `DROP TABLE`
explanation: What is `DROP TABLE`?
DROP TABLE is a DDL (Data Definition Language) command used to permanently remove an existing table from a database.
When a table is dropped, the database removes the table structure and the data stored in that table.
Definition: DROP TABLE removes an existing table and its stored data from the database.
Basic Syntax
DROP TABLE table_name;
For example:
DROP TABLE employees;
After this statement succeeds, the employees table no longer exists.

Before:
Database
   │
   ├── employees table
   │      ├── Columns
   │      └── Data
   │
   └── orders table

        DROP TABLE employees
                 ↓
After:
Database
   │
   └── orders table
What Does `DROP TABLE` Remove?

Object / DataWhat happens?
Table structureRemoved
RowsRemoved
ColumnsRemoved with the table
Table constraintsRemoved with the table
Indexes belonging to the tableRemoved as part of dropping the table, subject to database behavior
Table itselfRemoved
`DROP TABLE` vs `DELETE` vs `TRUNCATE`
These three commands are very important to distinguish.

CommandWhat happens?Table remains?
DELETERemoves selected rows or all rowsYes
TRUNCATE TABLERemoves all rowsYes
DROP TABLERemoves the table and its dataNo

DELETE
  ↓
Remove rows
  ↓
Table remains

TRUNCATE TABLE
  ↓
Remove all rows
  ↓
Table remains

DROP TABLE
  ↓
Remove table structure + data
  ↓
Table does not remain
1. `DROP TABLE` Removes the Entire Table
Suppose we have:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Now execute:
DROP TABLE employees;
The table definition and its stored rows are removed. A later query such as SELECT * FROM employees; will fail because the table no longer exists.
2. `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`
Many database systems support IF EXISTS with DROP TABLE.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS employees;
This is useful when a script should not fail simply because the table is already absent. Exact support and behavior can vary by database.
Important: IF EXISTS prevents an error for a missing table where supported. It does not make dropping an existing table safe.
3. Dropping Multiple Tables
Some database systems allow multiple tables to be dropped in one statement.
DROP TABLE table_a, table_b;
Because this syntax and dependency behavior can differ between database systems, check your database documentation before using it in production scripts.
4. What Happens to Data?
The data stored inside the dropped table is no longer available through that table because the table itself has been removed.

employees
──────────────
employee_id | name
101         | Rahul
102         | Priya
103         | Arun

       ↓ DROP TABLE

employees table
       ↓
    REMOVED
5. Foreign Key Dependencies
Dropping a table can be restricted when another table has a foreign key referencing it.

customers
──────────────
customer_id PK
      ↑
      │
      │ FK
      │
orders
──────────────
customer_id FK
For example, if orders.customer_id references customers.customer_id, attempting to drop customers may be rejected by the database unless the dependency is handled according to that database's rules.
DROP TABLE customers;
Do not assume that the database will automatically remove dependent objects. Dependency handling and options such as cascading are database-specific.
6. `DROP TABLE ... CASCADE`
Some databases support a CASCADE option that can remove dependent objects along with the table.
DROP TABLE customers CASCADE;
Danger: Cascading a drop can remove additional dependent database objects. Never use CASCADE casually in a production environment. First identify exactly what depends on the table.
7. `DROP TABLE` vs `DROP DATABASE`

CommandScope
DROP TABLERemoves one table
DROP DATABASERemoves an entire database where supported
DROP TABLE is destructive, but its scope is limited to the specified table and any dependencies affected by the database's drop rules.
8. `DROP TABLE` vs `ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN`

CommandResult
ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMNRemoves one or more columns from an existing table
DROP TABLERemoves the entire table

ALTER TABLE employees DROP COLUMN salary
                ↓
employees table remains
                ↓
Other columns still exist

DROP TABLE employees
                ↓
employees table is removed completely
9. Data Engineering Use Case: Temporary Staging Tables
Data Engineering pipelines sometimes create temporary or disposable staging tables during development, testing or controlled processing.

CREATE TABLE staging_orders (
    order_id INT,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
After the table is no longer required, it may be removed:
DROP TABLE staging_orders;
In production pipelines, whether a staging table should be dropped depends on the pipeline architecture, audit requirements, recovery strategy and database platform.
10. Data Engineering Use Case: Rebuilding Development Tables
During development, you may intentionally remove and recreate a table while changing its design.

DROP TABLE development_orders;

CREATE TABLE development_orders (
    order_id INT,
    customer_id INT,
    order_amount DECIMAL(12, 2),
    order_date DATE
);
This can be useful in development, but it is very different from safely evolving a production schema.
11. Production Safety
DROP TABLE should be treated as a high-risk operation in production.

Before DroppingCheck
Table nameConfirm the exact target table
DataDetermine whether the data is still required
DependenciesCheck foreign keys, views, procedures and applications
PipelinesCheck ETL/ELT jobs and downstream processes
ReportsCheck dashboards and BI queries
Backup/recoveryVerify that an appropriate recovery mechanism exists
EnvironmentConfirm you are connected to the intended database
12. Common Mistake: Dropping the Wrong Table
Before executing a destructive command, verify the current database and inspect the target table.

SELECT *
FROM employees;
After confirming the table is the correct target:
DROP TABLE employees;
Production Rule: Never execute a destructive DDL statement against a production table without first confirming the environment, object name, dependencies and recovery plan.
13. Common Mistakes

• Confusing DROP TABLE with DELETE.
  • Dropping a production table accidentally.
  • Using CASCADE without checking dependencies.
  • Assuming dropped data can always be recovered automatically.
  • Ignoring foreign key or view dependencies.
  • Running a DROP statement against the wrong database or schema.
  • Dropping a staging table that another pipeline still expects.
  • Using DROP when the actual requirement was only to remove rows.
Quick Summary

CommandMain Purpose
DROP TABLERemove an entire table and its data
DROP TABLE IF EXISTSDrop only if the table exists, where supported
DROP TABLE ... CASCADEDrop the table and dependent objects according to database rules
DELETERemove rows while keeping the table
TRUNCATE TABLERemove all rows while keeping the table structure
ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMNRemove a column while keeping the table
practice: Step 1: Create a sample employees table.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Step 2: Insert a few records into the table.

INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, employee_name, salary)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul', 35000),
    (102, 'Priya', 40000),
    (103, 'Arun', 45000);
Step 3: Verify that the table contains data.

SELECT *
FROM employees;
Step 4: Drop the table.
DROP TABLE employees;
Step 5: Try querying the table after dropping it and observe the database error.

SELECT *
FROM employees;
Step 6: Create a temporary development table and practice DROP TABLE IF EXISTS if your database supports it.

CREATE TABLE development_orders (
    order_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS development_orders;
Step 7: Compare the behavior of DELETE, TRUNCATE TABLE and DROP TABLE on separate practice tables. Do not perform this experiment on production data.
Step 8: Create customers and orders tables with a foreign key relationship. Try dropping the referenced table and observe how your database handles the dependency.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
Step 9: Before dropping a table in a real Data Engineering project, make a checklist of the ETL jobs, dashboards, applications and other tables that could depend on it.

Practice Goal: You should clearly understand that DROP TABLE removes the entire table and its data, know how it differs from DELETE and TRUNCATE TABLE, and understand why it is a high-risk operation in production Data Engineering environments.

qna.q: Q1. What is `DROP TABLE`?
qna.a: `DROP TABLE` is a DDL command that removes an existing table and its stored data from the database.

qna.q: Q2. Does the table remain after DROP TABLE?
qna.a: No. The table itself is removed.

qna.q: Q3. Does DROP TABLE remove the rows?
qna.a: Yes. Because the table itself is removed, the rows stored in that table are also removed.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between DROP TABLE and DELETE?
qna.a: `DELETE` removes rows while keeping the table. `DROP TABLE` removes the entire table.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE TABLE?
qna.a: `TRUNCATE TABLE` removes all rows but keeps the table structure. `DROP TABLE` removes both the data and the table structure.

qna.q: Q6. What does `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` do?
qna.a: Where supported, it drops the table only if it exists, preventing an error caused solely by the table being absent.

qna.q: Q7. What happens if another table has a foreign key referencing the table being dropped?
qna.a: The database may prevent the drop because of the dependency. The exact behavior and available options depend on the database system.

qna.q: Q8. What does CASCADE mean with DROP TABLE?
qna.a: In databases that support it, CASCADE allows dependent objects to be removed according to the database's dependency rules. It should be used carefully because it can have a wider impact than dropping the table alone.

qna.q: Q9. Can a dropped table always be recovered?
qna.a: No. Recovery depends on the database system, transaction behavior, backups, snapshots, point-in-time recovery and other operational mechanisms.

qna.q: Q10. Why is DROP TABLE dangerous in production?
qna.a: It can remove an entire table and its data, potentially breaking applications, reports, ETL pipelines and downstream data consumers.

qna.q: Q11. Can DROP TABLE remove indexes and constraints?
qna.a: Indexes and constraints belonging to the dropped table are removed as part of removing the table, subject to database-specific behavior.

qna.q: Q12. Is DROP TABLE a DDL command?
qna.a: Yes. `DROP TABLE` is generally classified as DDL because it changes the database schema.

qna.q: Q13. When might a Data Engineer use DROP TABLE?
qna.a: Common controlled uses include removing obsolete development tables, disposable staging structures or tables that are intentionally being replaced as part of a managed schema change.

qna.q: Q14. Should DROP TABLE be used for removing only rows?
qna.a: No. If the table must remain, use an appropriate row-removal operation such as `DELETE` or `TRUNCATE TABLE`, depending on the requirement and database behavior.

qna.q: Q15. What should you check before dropping a production table?
qna.a: Verify the database and schema, table name, data requirements, foreign keys and other dependencies, ETL pipelines, reports, applications, backups or recovery mechanisms, and the organization's change-management process.

items.title: `TRUNCATE TABLE`
explanation: What is `TRUNCATE TABLE`?
TRUNCATE TABLE is a SQL command used to remove all rows from an existing table while keeping the table structure.
Definition: TRUNCATE TABLE removes all rows from a table but keeps the table, columns, constraints and overall table definition available for future use.
Basic Syntax
TRUNCATE TABLE table_name;
Example:
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;
After this command, the employees table still exists, but its rows have been removed.

Before:
employees
────────────────────
employee_id | name
101         | Rahul
102         | Priya
103         | Arun

        ↓
TRUNCATE TABLE employees
        ↓

After:
employees
────────────────────
employee_id | name

Table structure remains
Rows = 0
What Does `TRUNCATE TABLE` Remove?

ItemResult
RowsRemoved
TableRemains
ColumnsRemain
Table definitionRemains
IndexesGenerally remain as part of the table structure, subject to database behavior
ConstraintsGenerally remain, subject to database behavior
`TRUNCATE TABLE` vs `DELETE` vs `DROP TABLE`

CommandRowsTable StructureMain Purpose
DELETESelected rows or all rowsRemainsRemove data with row-level filtering
TRUNCATE TABLEAll rowsRemainsQuickly empty a table
DROP TABLERemovedRemovedRemove the entire table

DELETE
  ↓
Remove rows
  ↓
Table remains
  ↓
WHERE can usually be used

TRUNCATE TABLE
  ↓
Remove all rows
  ↓
Table remains
  ↓
No WHERE clause

DROP TABLE
  ↓
Remove rows + table structure
  ↓
Table does not remain
1. TRUNCATE Removes All Rows
Suppose the table contains:

SELECT *
FROM employees;
Result:

employee_id | employee_name | salary
------------+---------------+-------
101         | Rahul         | 35000
102         | Priya         | 40000
103         | Arun          | 45000
Now run:
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;
The table still exists, but it contains no rows.
2. `TRUNCATE` Does Not Use `WHERE`
You cannot use WHERE with the normal TRUNCATE TABLE statement.
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;
This removes all rows.
If you need to remove only specific rows, use DELETE.

DELETE FROM employees
WHERE salary < 30000;
Remember: DELETE can normally filter rows with WHERE. TRUNCATE TABLE is an all-rows operation.
3. The Table Can Be Used Again
After truncating a table, you can insert new records into the same table.

TRUNCATE TABLE employees;

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, salary)
VALUES
    (201, 'Kiran', 42000);
The table definition was not removed, so the table can continue to be used.
4. Why Use TRUNCATE?
TRUNCATE TABLE is useful when you want to completely empty a table while keeping its structure.

SituationSuitable?
Remove a few selected rowsUse DELETE
Remove all rows and keep tableUse TRUNCATE TABLE
Remove table completelyUse DROP TABLE
5. Data Engineering Example: Staging Table
Staging tables are commonly used during ETL/ELT processing.

Source Files / API
        ↓
   Staging Table
        ↓
 Transformation
        ↓
 Target Table
Suppose a staging table is reused for each controlled load. After processing the current batch, the staging table may need to be emptied before the next batch.
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders;
The staging table remains available for the next load.
6. TRUNCATE in an ETL Workflow

Previous staging data
        ↓
TRUNCATE TABLE
        ↓
Empty staging table
        ↓
Load new source data
        ↓
Transform / Validate
        ↓
Load target table
This pattern can be useful for a full-refresh staging workflow, but it is not appropriate for every pipeline. Incremental pipelines often need to preserve historical or unprocessed data.
7. TRUNCATE and Auto-Increment / Identity Values
Some database systems reset identity or auto-increment counters when a table is truncated, while others have different behavior or options.
Therefore, do not assume that the next generated ID will always restart at 1 after a truncate.
Database Note: Identity/sequence behavior after TRUNCATE is database-specific. Always check the behavior of the database you are using.
8. TRUNCATE and Transactions
The transactional behavior of TRUNCATE TABLE varies between database systems. Some systems allow it to participate in transactions and be rolled back, while others have different rules.
For example, do not assume that this behavior is identical across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle.
Important: Whether TRUNCATE can be rolled back, how locks work, and how logging is handled are database-specific topics. Learn these details when studying the corresponding database platform.
9. TRUNCATE and Performance
TRUNCATE TABLE is generally designed for efficiently removing all rows without processing each row in the same way as a typical DELETE.
However, performance and internal implementation depend on the database system, table design, indexes, constraints and storage engine.
Data Engineering Tip: Think of TRUNCATE primarily as a schema-preserving full-table reset, not simply as a universally faster version of DELETE.
10. TRUNCATE and Foreign Keys
Foreign key relationships can affect whether a table can be truncated.

customers
──────────────
customer_id PK
      ↑
      │ FK
      │
orders
──────────────
customer_id FK
If another table references the table being truncated, the database may restrict the operation or require special handling. The exact rules vary by database.
11. TRUNCATE vs DELETE for Data Engineering

RequirementRecommended Concept
Remove specific invalid recordsDELETE ... WHERE
Remove all records from a reusable staging tableTRUNCATE TABLE may be appropriate
Remove an obsolete table completelyDROP TABLE
Keep historical recordsDo not blindly truncate
Incremental pipelineUsually requires more careful data-retention logic
12. Production Safety
TRUNCATE TABLE is destructive because it removes every row from the target table.

Check Before TruncatingWhy?
Database/environmentAvoid truncating the wrong environment
Table nameConfirm the exact target
Data importanceAll rows will be removed
Pipeline dependenciesOther jobs may expect the data
Downstream reportsDashboards may temporarily or permanently lose data
Recovery planUnderstand how the database handles recovery
13. Common Mistakes

• Using TRUNCATE when only a few rows should be removed.
  • Expecting WHERE to work with TRUNCATE TABLE.
  • Confusing TRUNCATE TABLE with DROP TABLE.
  • Assuming identity or auto-increment behavior is identical across databases.
  • Assuming transaction and rollback behavior is identical across databases.
  • Truncating a production staging or target table without checking active pipelines.
  • Assuming all foreign-key scenarios behave the same across database systems.
  • Forgetting that every row in the table will be removed.
Quick Summary

CommandRowsTableWHERE
DELETESelected or allRemainsNormally supported
TRUNCATE TABLEAllRemainsNo
DROP TABLERemoved with tableRemovedNo
Remember: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE TABLE empties the table while keeping its structure, and DROP TABLE removes the table itself.
practice: Step 1: Create a practice employees table.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Step 2: Insert several records.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, salary)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul', 35000),
    (102, 'Priya', 40000),
    (103, 'Arun', 45000);
Step 3: Verify the number of rows.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows
FROM employees;
Step 4: Truncate the table.
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;
Step 5: Verify that the table contains zero rows.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows
FROM employees;
Step 6: Verify that the table structure still exists by inserting a new record.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, salary)
VALUES
    (201, 'Kiran', 42000);
Step 7: Retrieve the new record.

SELECT *
FROM employees;
Step 8: Create a staging table similar to a Data Engineering pipeline.

CREATE TABLE staging_orders (
    order_id INT,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
Step 9: Insert sample staging data.

INSERT INTO staging_orders
    (order_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES
    (1, 101, 1500),
    (2, 102, 2500),
    (3, 103, 3200);
Step 10: Simulate the beginning of a new full-refresh staging load by truncating the staging table.
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders;
Step 11: Compare the commands by creating separate practice tables and observing the result of DELETE, TRUNCATE TABLE and DROP TABLE. Perform this only with test data.
Step 12: Write down which operation you would choose for each situation: remove one invalid row, empty an entire reusable staging table, or permanently remove an obsolete table.

Practice Goal: You should be able to explain why TRUNCATE TABLE removes all rows while preserving the table structure, understand how it differs from DELETE and DROP TABLE, and recognize its practical use in full-refresh Data Engineering staging workflows.

qna.q: Q1. What is `TRUNCATE TABLE`?
qna.a: `TRUNCATE TABLE` removes all rows from an existing table while keeping the table structure.

qna.q: Q2. Does TRUNCATE remove the table?
qna.a: No. The table remains and can be used again.

qna.q: Q3. Does TRUNCATE remove all rows?
qna.a: Yes. `TRUNCATE TABLE` is an all-rows operation.

qna.q: Q4. Can you use WHERE with TRUNCATE TABLE?
qna.a: No. Normal `TRUNCATE TABLE` does not support a WHERE clause. Use `DELETE ... WHERE` when only specific rows should be removed.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
qna.a: `DELETE` can normally remove selected rows using WHERE, while `TRUNCATE TABLE` removes all rows from the table.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DROP TABLE?
qna.a: `TRUNCATE TABLE` removes all rows but keeps the table. `DROP TABLE` removes the table itself along with its data.

qna.q: Q7. Is TRUNCATE a DDL command?
qna.a: `TRUNCATE TABLE` is generally classified as a DDL or schema-level operation, but exact transactional and implementation behavior is database-specific.

qna.q: Q8. Is TRUNCATE always faster than DELETE?
qna.a: It is often designed to remove all rows more efficiently than a row-by-row DELETE, but actual performance depends on the database system and table design.

qna.q: Q9. Can TRUNCATE be rolled back?
qna.a: The answer depends on the database system and transaction behavior. Do not assume identical rollback behavior across different databases.

qna.q: Q10. Does TRUNCATE reset auto-increment or identity values?
qna.a: It can, but the behavior is database-specific. Always check the documentation for the database you are using.

qna.q: Q11. Why is TRUNCATE useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can be useful for emptying reusable staging tables before a controlled full-refresh load while keeping the table structure.

qna.q: Q12. Should TRUNCATE be used in an incremental pipeline?
qna.a: Not blindly. Incremental pipelines usually need to preserve existing data, so truncating the target or staging table may destroy information required for the incremental process.

qna.q: Q13. What happens to constraints after TRUNCATE?
qna.a: The table remains with its structure and constraints generally remaining in place, although exact behavior can vary by database system.

qna.q: Q14. What happens if another table references the table being truncated?
qna.a: The database may restrict the operation or require special handling. Foreign-key behavior is database-specific.

qna.q: Q15. When should you use DELETE instead of TRUNCATE?
qna.a: Use `DELETE` when you need to remove selected rows, use a WHERE condition, or otherwise need row-level deletion semantics.

qna.q: Q16. When should you use DROP TABLE instead?
qna.a: Use `DROP TABLE` when the entire table is no longer required and you intentionally want to remove its structure and data.

items.title: `PRIMARY KEY`
explanation: What is a `PRIMARY KEY`?
A PRIMARY KEY is a constraint used to uniquely identify each row in a table.
Definition: A primary key is a column or combination of columns whose values uniquely identify every row in a table. A primary key cannot contain NULL values and must be unique.
Why Do We Need a Primary Key?
Consider an employees table:

employee_id | employee_name | department
------------+---------------+------------
101         | Rahul         | IT
102         | Priya         | HR
103         | Arun          | Finance
The employee_id can uniquely identify each employee.

Employee Table

employee_id
     ↓
101 ─────────→ Rahul
102 ─────────→ Priya
103 ─────────→ Arun

Each employee_id identifies exactly one row.
Primary Key Rules

RuleMeaning
UniqueNo two rows can have the same primary-key value.
Not NULLA primary-key value cannot be NULL.
One primary keyA table can have only one primary-key constraint.
Can contain multiple columnsA primary key can be a composite key.
Identifies a rowIt provides the table's main row identity.
1. Creating a Primary Key During Table Creation
The simplest approach is to define the primary key when creating the table.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Here, employee_id is the primary key.
2. Primary Key with a Named Constraint
You can explicitly give the primary-key constraint a name.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2),
    CONSTRAINT pk_employees PRIMARY KEY (employee_id)
);
Naming constraints can make database administration and troubleshooting easier.
3. Adding a Primary Key to an Existing Table
You can add a primary key to an existing table using ALTER TABLE, provided the existing data satisfies the primary-key requirements.

ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT pk_employees
PRIMARY KEY (employee_id);
This operation can fail if employee_id contains duplicate or NULL values.
4. Primary Key Must Be Unique
The following data is valid:

employee_id | employee_name
------------+--------------
101         | Rahul
102         | Priya
103         | Arun
This is invalid if employee_id is the primary key:

employee_id | employee_name
------------+--------------
101         | Rahul
101         | Priya
The database rejects the second row because two rows cannot have the same primary-key value.
5. Primary Key Cannot Be NULL
A primary key must identify a real row, so it cannot contain NULL.

INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, employee_name)
VALUES (NULL, 'Rahul');
If employee_id is the primary key, this insert will be rejected.
Remember: Primary key = Unique + NOT NULL.
6. Primary Key vs UNIQUE Constraint

FeaturePRIMARY KEYUNIQUE
Duplicates allowed?NoNo
NULL allowed?NoDatabase-specific behavior
How many per table?One primary-key constraintCan have multiple UNIQUE constraints
Main purposeIdentify each rowEnforce uniqueness
For example, an employee table might use employee_id as the primary key and email as a separate unique constraint.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);
7. Primary Key vs Foreign Key
These two concepts are closely related in relational databases.

customers
──────────────────
customer_id PK
customer_name
       │
       │ referenced by
       ↓
orders
──────────────────
order_id PK
customer_id FK

KeyPurpose
PRIMARY KEYUniquely identifies a row in its own table
FOREIGN KEYReferences a key in another table to represent a relationship
8. Primary Key and Foreign Key Example

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
Here:

• customers.customer_id is the primary key.
  • orders.order_id is the primary key.
  • orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing the customer.
9. Composite Primary Key
A primary key does not have to contain only one column. Two or more columns can work together as the primary key.
This is called a composite primary key.

CREATE TABLE student_courses (
    student_id INT,
    course_id INT,
    enrollment_date DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
Here, neither student_id nor course_id has to be unique by itself. The combination of both must be unique.

student_id | course_id
------------+----------
101         | 10
101         | 20
102         | 10
The combination (101, 10) cannot appear again.
10. Why Composite Keys Are Useful in Data Engineering
Composite keys are common in relationship or bridge tables where a row represents a combination of entities.

Student ───────┐
               │
               ↓
        Student_Course
        ┌───────────────┐
        │ student_id   │
        │ course_id    │
        └───────────────┘
               ↑
               │
Course ────────┘
For example, one student can enroll in many courses and one course can contain many students.
11. Choosing a Good Primary Key
A good primary key should provide a stable and reliable way to identify a row.

CharacteristicWhy it matters
UniqueEach row can be distinguished.
Not NULLEvery row has an identity.
StableThe identifier should not normally change.
MinimalAvoid unnecessary columns in the key.
ReliableThe value should not depend on frequently changing business information.
12. Natural Key vs Surrogate Key
In Data Engineering and database design, you will often encounter two approaches to identifying records.

TypeMeaningExample
Natural KeyAn identifier that already exists in the business dataGovernment-issued customer number or business-defined product code
Surrogate KeyAn artificial identifier created specifically for the databaseGenerated integer or UUID
For example:
customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY
The customer_id could be a surrogate key generated by the system. The exact choice depends on the data model and system requirements.
13. Auto-Generated Primary Keys
Many databases support mechanisms for automatically generating identifiers. The syntax differs between database systems.
A generic example is:

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
The application or database sequence/identity mechanism can generate order_id values. The exact implementation is database-specific.

Data Engineering Tip: Do not assume that every database generates primary keys in the same way. PostgreSQL sequences/identity columns, SQL Server identity columns, Oracle identity/sequence approaches and MySQL auto-increment have different syntax and behavior.
14. Primary Key and Data Quality
Primary keys are important for data quality because they help detect duplicate or missing identifiers.

Incoming Data
     ↓
Validate Primary Key
     ↓
┌───────────────┐
│ Unique?       │
│ Not NULL?     │
└───────┬───────┘
        ↓
   Valid / Invalid
        ↓
Target Table
In a Data Engineering pipeline, duplicate or NULL business identifiers may indicate upstream data-quality problems.
15. Primary Key and Duplicate Data
Suppose an ingestion pipeline receives:

customer_id | customer_name
------------+--------------
101         | Rahul
102         | Priya
101         | Rahul Kumar
If customer_id is the primary key of the target table, the two records with ID 101 cannot both be inserted into that table.
A Data Engineering pipeline must decide what the duplicate means. It could represent an error, an update, a late-arriving record or a legitimate source-system event depending on the business rules.
16. Primary Key and Table Grain
Understanding the grain of a table is important before choosing a primary key.
Table Grain: The grain describes what one row in a table represents.
For example, if one row represents one order:

orders

order_id = one unique order
Then order_id may be a suitable primary key.
But if one row represents one product within an order:

order_items

order_id + product_id = one order item combination
A composite key or another unique identifier may be more appropriate depending on the data model.
17. Removing a Primary Key
A named primary-key constraint can generally be removed using ALTER TABLE, but the exact syntax depends on the database.

ALTER TABLE employees
DROP CONSTRAINT pk_employees;
Removing the primary key can affect foreign keys, applications, data quality and downstream processes, so it should be carefully evaluated.
18. Common Mistakes

• Allowing duplicate values in a column intended to identify rows.
  • Trying to insert NULL into a primary-key column.
  • Choosing a frequently changing business value as the identifier without considering the consequences.
  • Ignoring the table grain when choosing a primary key.
  • Assuming every table must use an integer primary key.
  • Confusing a primary key with a foreign key.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide duplicate-key problems instead of fixing the underlying data issue.
  • Adding a primary key to existing data without checking for duplicates and NULLs.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
PRIMARY KEYUniquely identifies rows
UniqueDuplicate primary-key values are not allowed
NOT NULLPrimary-key values cannot be NULL
Composite KeyMultiple columns together form the primary key
Foreign KeyReferences a key in another table
Data EngineeringUseful for data integrity, relationships and identifying records
Remember: A primary key answers one fundamental question: "Which row is this?"
practice: Step 1: Create an employees table with employee_id as the primary key.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    department VARCHAR(50),
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Step 2: Insert valid records with unique employee IDs.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul', 'IT', 35000),
    (102, 'Priya', 'HR', 40000),
    (103, 'Arun', 'Finance', 45000);
Step 3: Try inserting a duplicate primary-key value and observe the database error.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES
    (101, 'Kiran', 'IT', 42000);
Step 4: Try inserting a NULL primary-key value and observe the result.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES
    (NULL, 'Kiran', 'IT', 42000);
Step 5: Create a customers table and make customer_id the primary key.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150)
);
Step 6: Create an orders table with its own primary key and a customer ID column.

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);
Step 7: Create a foreign-key relationship from orders to customers.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
Step 8: Practice a composite primary key using a student-course relationship table.

CREATE TABLE student_courses (
    student_id INT,
    course_id INT,
    enrollment_date DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
Step 9: Insert valid combinations into the composite-key table.

INSERT INTO student_courses
    (student_id, course_id, enrollment_date)
VALUES
    (101, 10, '2026-01-10'),
    (101, 20, '2026-01-11'),
    (102, 10, '2026-01-12');
Step 10: Try inserting the same student_id + course_id combination again and observe the primary-key violation.

INSERT INTO student_courses
    (student_id, course_id, enrollment_date)
VALUES
    (101, 10, '2026-02-01');
Step 11: Think like a Data Engineer. For an orders table, decide what one row represents and explain why order_id can uniquely identify it.
Step 12: Take a sample staging dataset and identify whether its intended primary key contains duplicates or NULL values before loading it into a target table.

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a primary key, understand uniqueness and NOT NULL requirements, use composite primary keys, connect primary and foreign keys, and recognize how primary keys support data quality and Data Engineering table design.

qna.q: Q1. What is a PRIMARY KEY?
qna.a: A primary key is a column or combination of columns that uniquely identifies every row in a table.

qna.q: Q2. Can a primary key contain duplicate values?
qna.a: No. Primary-key values must be unique.

qna.q: Q3. Can a primary key contain NULL?
qna.a: No. A primary key cannot contain NULL values.

qna.q: Q4. How many primary keys can a table have?
qna.a: A table can have only one primary-key constraint, although that constraint can contain multiple columns.

qna.q: Q5. What is a composite primary key?
qna.a: A composite primary key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.

qna.q: Q6. Can each column in a composite primary key contain duplicate values?
qna.a: Yes. Individual columns can contain duplicate values as long as the combination of all columns in the composite key remains unique.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?
qna.a: Both enforce uniqueness, but a table can have only one primary-key constraint while it can have multiple UNIQUE constraints. NULL behavior for UNIQUE constraints varies by database.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY?
qna.a: A primary key identifies rows in its own table. A foreign key references a key in another table to represent a relationship.

qna.q: Q9. Why is a primary key important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It helps identify records, enforce uniqueness, establish relationships and detect duplicate or invalid records during data processing.

qna.q: Q10. What happens if you insert a duplicate primary-key value?
qna.a: The database normally rejects the insert because it would violate the primary-key uniqueness constraint.

qna.q: Q11. What happens if you insert NULL into a primary-key column?
qna.a: The database rejects the operation because primary-key columns cannot contain NULL.

qna.q: Q12. What is a surrogate key?
qna.a: A surrogate key is an artificial identifier created specifically for a data model, such as a generated integer or UUID.

qna.q: Q13. What is a natural key?
qna.a: A natural key is an identifier that already exists as part of the business data and can uniquely identify an entity.

qna.q: Q14. What is table grain and why does it matter for a primary key?
qna.a: Table grain describes what one row represents. Understanding the grain helps determine which column or combination of columns should uniquely identify that row.

qna.q: Q15. Can a primary key be added after a table has been created?
qna.a: Yes. You can use ALTER TABLE to add a primary-key constraint, provided the existing data satisfies the required uniqueness and non-NULL rules.

qna.q: Q16. Can a primary key be removed?
qna.a: Yes, a primary-key constraint can generally be removed using ALTER TABLE, but doing so may affect foreign keys and downstream applications or pipelines.

items.title: `FOREIGN KEY`
explanation: What is a `FOREIGN KEY`?
A FOREIGN KEY is a constraint used to create a relationship between tables by referencing a key in another table.
Definition: A foreign key is a column or combination of columns in one table that references a candidate key, commonly a primary key, in another table.
Why Do We Need a Foreign Key?
Relational databases store related information in separate tables. A foreign key connects those tables.
For example, instead of storing customer information repeatedly inside every order, we can keep customers and orders in separate tables.

customers
──────────────────
customer_id PK
customer_name
      │
      │ referenced by
      ↓
orders
──────────────────
order_id PK
customer_id FK
amount
Here, orders.customer_id references customers.customer_id.
Basic Syntax

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
The general relationship is:

Parent Table
    │
    │ Primary Key
    ↓
Child Table
    │
    │ Foreign Key
    └──────────────→ references Parent Key
1. Parent Table and Child Table
The table containing the referenced key is commonly called the parent or referenced table.
The table containing the foreign key is commonly called the child or referencing table.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);

TableKeyRole
customerscustomer_idReferenced / Parent key
orderscustomer_idForeign / Child key
2. Foreign Key Values Must Match the Referenced Key
Suppose the customers table contains:

customer_id | customer_name
------------+--------------
101         | Rahul
102         | Priya
103         | Arun
This order is valid because customer 101 exists:

INSERT INTO orders
    (order_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES
    (5001, 101, 1500);
But this can be rejected:

INSERT INTO orders
    (order_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES
    (5002, 999, 2500);
If customer 999 does not exist in the referenced table, the foreign-key constraint normally prevents the insert.
Remember: A foreign key helps prevent a child row from referring to a non-existent parent row.
3. Foreign Key Does Not Have to Be Unique
This is an important difference between a primary key and a foreign key.
Multiple orders can belong to the same customer.
The value 101 appears multiple times in orders.customer_id. This is valid because a foreign key does not normally require uniqueness.

Customer 101
     │
     ├──── Order 5001
     ├──── Order 5002
     └──── Order 5004

One customer → many orders
4. Foreign Key vs Primary Key

FeaturePRIMARY KEYFOREIGN KEY
Main purposeUniquely identifies a rowCreates a relationship between tables
DuplicatesNot allowedUsually allowed
NULLNot allowedMay be allowed unless restricted by NOT NULL
References another table?Not necessarilyYes
How many per table?One primary-key constraintMultiple foreign-key constraints can exist
5. Foreign Key Can Reference a Primary Key
The most common design is for a foreign key to reference the primary key of another table.

CREATE TABLE departments (
    department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    department_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (department_id)
        REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);

departments
───────────────
department_id PK
       │
       │ referenced by
       ↓
employees
───────────────
employee_id PK
department_id FK
6. A Foreign Key Can Reference a UNIQUE Key
Depending on the database and constraint rules, a foreign key can reference a candidate key such as a UNIQUE key, not only a primary key.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);
A child table may reference an eligible unique key according to the database's foreign-key rules.

Practical Rule: For beginner-level relational design, think of a foreign key as normally referencing the primary key of the parent table. More advanced database designs can use other candidate keys where supported.
7. Adding a Foreign Key After Table Creation
You can add a foreign-key constraint to an existing table using ALTER TABLE.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
The existing data must satisfy the foreign-key relationship before the constraint can be added successfully.
8. Foreign Key and NULL
A foreign-key column can often contain NULL if the column is not defined as NOT NULL.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    manager_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (manager_id)
        REFERENCES employees(employee_id)
);
A NULL manager_id can represent an employee who currently has no manager, assuming the column permits NULL.

Important: NULL in a foreign-key column generally means there is no referenced value for that row. It is different from referencing a parent row whose key value is missing, which a foreign-key constraint is designed to prevent.
9. Foreign Key and Referential Integrity
The main purpose of a foreign key is to help maintain referential integrity.
Referential Integrity: A database integrity rule that helps ensure relationships between related tables remain valid.

customers
101 | Rahul
102 | Priya

        ↓

orders
5001 | 101 | 1500  ✓
5002 | 102 | 2500  ✓
5003 | 999 | 3000  ✗

999 does not exist in customers.
The foreign key helps prevent the invalid relationship represented by customer 999.
10. What Happens When a Parent Row Is Deleted?
Suppose:

customers
customer_id = 101

orders
order_id = 5001
customer_id = 101
Now you try to delete customer 101.

DELETE FROM customers
WHERE customer_id = 101;
If the order still references customer 101, the database may reject the deletion because it would leave an invalid child reference. The exact behavior depends on the foreign-key action defined.
11. `ON DELETE CASCADE`
Some database systems allow you to define an action such as ON DELETE CASCADE.

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE
);
With this rule, deleting a parent customer can automatically delete related child rows according to the database's foreign-key behavior.
Warning: Cascading deletes can remove many related rows automatically. Use them only when that behavior matches the business requirement.
12. `ON DELETE SET NULL`
Another possible action is ON DELETE SET NULL, where supported.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    manager_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (manager_id)
        REFERENCES employees(employee_id)
        ON DELETE SET NULL
);
When the referenced parent row is deleted, the child foreign-key value can be set to NULL, provided the column allows NULL and the database supports the action.
13. Common Foreign-Key Actions

ActionConcept
NO ACTION / RESTRICTPrevent or restrict the parent change when dependent rows exist, subject to database behavior.
CASCADEPropagate the parent change to related child rows.
SET NULLSet the child foreign-key value to NULL.
SET DEFAULTSet the child value to its default where supported and valid.
14. One-to-Many Relationship
Foreign keys are commonly used to represent one-to-many relationships.

One Customer
     │
     ├──────── Order 1
     ├──────── Order 2
     ├──────── Order 3
     └──────── Order 4

customers.customer_id
        ↓
orders.customer_id
One customer can have many orders, while each order belongs to one customer in this model.
15. One-to-One Relationship
A foreign key can also participate in a one-to-one relationship when the foreign-key column is additionally constrained to be unique.

CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE user_profiles (
    profile_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT UNIQUE,
    FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES users(user_id)
);
The UNIQUE constraint prevents multiple profile rows from referencing the same user, subject to the database's NULL behavior.
16. Many-to-Many Relationship
A many-to-many relationship is commonly implemented using a bridge or junction table containing foreign keys to both entities.

students              courses
──────────             ──────────
student_id PK          course_id PK
     │                      │
     │                      │
     └──────────┬───────────┘
                ↓
        student_courses
        ────────────────
        student_id FK
        course_id FK
For example, one student can take many courses and one course can contain many students.
17. Foreign Keys in Data Engineering

Foreign keys are useful for expressing relationships and enforcing integrity in relational systems. However, large analytical warehouses and distributed data platforms may not always enforce them physically.

Source System
     ↓
Customer Data ───────→ customers
     ↓
Order Data ──────────→ orders
                           │
                           │ customer_id
                           ↓
                    customers.customer_id
Even when physical foreign-key constraints are not enforced, Data Engineers still need to understand the logical relationship between keys to perform correct joins, validation and reconciliation.
18. Foreign Key and Data Quality
Foreign-key relationships can help identify orphan records.
Orphan Record: A child record whose supposed parent record does not exist.
For example, an order referencing a customer ID that does not exist is an orphan relationship.

SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
This is a useful Data Engineering validation pattern for detecting missing parent records, even in systems where foreign keys are not physically enforced.
19. Foreign Key and JOINs
Foreign keys often provide the logical relationship used when joining tables.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    c.customer_name,
    o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
The foreign-key relationship does not automatically perform the JOIN. It simply defines a relationship between the columns. The query still needs an explicit JOIN when you want to combine the data.
20. Common Mistakes

• Thinking a foreign key must contain unique values.
  • Confusing a foreign key with a primary key.
  • Inserting a child value that has no matching parent.
  • Deleting parent rows without understanding dependent child rows.
  • Using ON DELETE CASCADE without understanding its impact.
  • Forgetting that NULL may be allowed in a foreign-key column unless restricted.
  • Assuming every Data Warehouse physically enforces foreign keys.
  • Joining tables without understanding the relationship and table grain.
  • Assuming a foreign key automatically performs a JOIN.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
FOREIGN KEYCreates a relationship to a key in another table
Parent TableContains the referenced key
Child TableContains the foreign key
Referential IntegrityHelps keep table relationships valid
Duplicate FK valuesNormally allowed
NULL FK valuesMay be allowed if the column is nullable
ON DELETE CASCADECan propagate parent deletion to child rows
Data EngineeringUseful for relationships, joins, validation and reconciliation
Remember: A primary key answers "Which row is this?". A foreign key answers "Which row in another table is this related to?".
practice: Step 1: Create a customers table with customer_id as the primary key.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);
Step 2: Create an orders table containing a foreign key referencing customers.

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
Step 3: Insert valid customers.

INSERT INTO customers
    (customer_id, customer_name)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul'),
    (102, 'Priya'),
    (103, 'Arun');
Step 4: Insert orders whose customer IDs exist in the customers table.

INSERT INTO orders
    (order_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES
    (5001, 101, 1500),
    (5002, 101, 2500),
    (5003, 102, 3000);
Step 5: Try inserting an order for a customer that does not exist.

INSERT INTO orders
    (order_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES
    (5004, 999, 4000);
Step 6: Observe the foreign-key violation produced by your database.
Step 7: Use the foreign-key relationship to join customers and orders.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    c.customer_name,
    o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Step 8: Detect orphan customer references using a LEFT JOIN. In a properly enforced foreign-key relationship, this query should normally return no rows.

SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
Step 9: Create an employee-manager self-referencing relationship using a foreign key.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    manager_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (manager_id)
        REFERENCES employees(employee_id)
);
Step 10: Create a student-course junction table with two foreign keys and a composite primary key.

CREATE TABLE students (
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    student_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE courses (
    course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    course_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE student_courses (
    student_id INT,
    course_id INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(student_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES courses(course_id)
);
Step 11: Think like a Data Engineer. Take an orders dataset and identify which column should reference the customer table. Explain what should happen if an order contains an unknown customer ID.
Step 12: Create a small staging dataset containing an invalid customer ID and write a validation query that identifies the invalid relationship before loading the target table.

Practice Goal: You should be able to create foreign-key relationships, understand parent and child tables, distinguish primary keys from foreign keys, detect invalid relationships, understand cascading actions, and use key relationships correctly in Data Engineering joins and data-quality checks.

qna.q: Q1. What is a FOREIGN KEY?
qna.a: A foreign key is a column or combination of columns that references a key in another table and helps maintain a valid relationship between the tables.

qna.q: Q2. What is the parent table?
qna.a: The parent or referenced table is the table containing the key that is referenced by the foreign key.

qna.q: Q3. What is the child table?
qna.a: The child or referencing table is the table containing the foreign-key column.

qna.q: Q4. Can a foreign key contain duplicate values?
qna.a: Yes. Foreign-key values normally do not have to be unique. For example, many orders can belong to the same customer.

qna.q: Q5. Can a foreign key contain NULL?
qna.a: Yes, if the foreign-key column allows NULL and the database's constraint rules permit it.

qna.q: Q6. What is referential integrity?
qna.a: Referential integrity is the rule that helps ensure relationships between related tables remain valid.

qna.q: Q7. Can a foreign key reference a primary key?
qna.a: Yes. This is the most common foreign-key design.

qna.q: Q8. Can a foreign key reference a UNIQUE key?
qna.a: Depending on the database and key definition, a foreign key can reference an eligible unique candidate key.

qna.q: Q9. What happens when a foreign key references a value that does not exist?
qna.a: If the foreign-key constraint is enforced, the database normally rejects the operation that would create the invalid reference.

qna.q: Q10. What is ON DELETE CASCADE?
qna.a: It is a foreign-key action that can automatically delete related child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted, where supported and configured.

qna.q: Q11. What is ON DELETE SET NULL?
qna.a: It can set the child foreign-key value to NULL when the referenced parent row is deleted, provided the column allows NULL and the database supports the action.

qna.q: Q12. Does a foreign key automatically perform a JOIN?
qna.a: No. A foreign key defines a relationship. You still write an explicit JOIN when you want to retrieve combined data.

qna.q: Q13. How is a foreign key useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It helps model relationships, support correct joins, enforce integrity in relational systems and identify invalid or orphan relationships during data validation.

qna.q: Q14. What is an orphan record?
qna.a: An orphan record is a child record whose referenced parent record does not exist.

qna.q: Q15. Can one table have multiple foreign keys?
qna.a: Yes. A table can have multiple foreign-key constraints referencing the same or different tables.

qna.q: Q16. What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY?
qna.a: A primary key uniquely identifies a row in its own table. A foreign key references a key in another table to represent a relationship.

qna.q: Q17. How can a foreign key represent a one-to-many relationship?
qna.a: The parent table has one row identified by its key, while multiple child rows can contain the same foreign-key value referencing that parent.

qna.q: Q18. How is a many-to-many relationship commonly implemented?
qna.a: A junction or bridge table is used with foreign keys referencing both related tables, often with a composite primary key.

items.title: `UNIQUE`
explanation: What is `UNIQUE`?
UNIQUE is a SQL constraint used to ensure that values in a column, or combination of columns, are not duplicated according to the database's uniqueness rules.
Definition: A UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate values for the constrained column or column combination.
Why Do We Need `UNIQUE`?
Some columns should contain unique business values even though they are not the table's primary key.
For example, an employee may have a primary key called employee_id, while the employee's company email should also be unique.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);
Here:

• employee_id uniquely identifies the row as the primary key.
  • email must not be duplicated according to the UNIQUE constraint.

employees
────────────────────────
employee_id  → PRIMARY KEY
email        → UNIQUE

Primary Key:
Identifies the row

UNIQUE:
Prevents duplicate values
1. Creating a UNIQUE Constraint on a Column
The simplest syntax is to define UNIQUE next to the column.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);
Now two rows cannot normally have the same email value.
2. Named UNIQUE Constraint
You can explicitly name the constraint.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150),
    CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email UNIQUE (email)
);
Naming constraints is useful when you need to identify, modify or troubleshoot them later.
3. Adding UNIQUE to an Existing Table
You can add a unique constraint to an existing table using ALTER TABLE.

ALTER TABLE customers
ADD CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email
UNIQUE (email);
This can fail if existing data already contains duplicate values.
4. Duplicate Values Are Rejected
Suppose the table contains:

customer_id | customer_name | email
------------+---------------+--------------------
101         | Rahul         | rahul@example.com
102         | Priya         | priya@example.com
This insert would normally violate the unique constraint:

INSERT INTO customers
    (customer_id, customer_name, email)
VALUES
    (103, 'Arun', 'rahul@example.com');
The email already exists, so the database rejects the duplicate according to the constraint rules.
Remember: UNIQUE is about preventing duplicate values. It does not mean that the column is automatically the table's primary key.
5. `UNIQUE` vs `PRIMARY KEY`

FeaturePRIMARY KEYUNIQUE
PurposeIdentifies each rowEnforces uniqueness
Duplicate valuesNot allowedNot allowed
NULL behaviorNot allowedDatabase-specific
Number per tableOne primary-key constraintMultiple UNIQUE constraints can exist
Can be composite?YesYes
For example:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE,
    phone_number VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE
);
This table has one primary key and two separate unique constraints.
6. Can a UNIQUE Column Contain NULL?
This is an important database-specific detail.

Unlike a primary key, a UNIQUE constraint does not universally have the same NULL behavior across all database systems. Some databases allow one or more NULL values in a UNIQUE column because NULL represents an unknown value, while other systems or configurations may behave differently.
Important: Never assume that NULL behavior for UNIQUE is identical across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and other databases. Check the behavior of the database you are using.
7. Composite UNIQUE Constraint
A UNIQUE constraint can contain multiple columns. In that case, the combination of the columns must be unique.

CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id INT,
    course_id INT,
    enrollment_date DATE,
    CONSTRAINT uq_student_course
        UNIQUE (student_id, course_id)
);
Here, the individual values do not have to be unique.

student_id | course_id
------------+----------
101         | 10
101         | 20
102         | 10
But this combination cannot appear again:

student_id | course_id
------------+----------
101         | 10
The pair (101, 10) already exists.
8. `UNIQUE` and Table Grain
Understanding table grain helps you decide what should be unique.
Table Grain: The grain describes what one row in a table represents.
Suppose one row represents one employee. The company email may be unique:

employee_id | email
------------+-------------------
101         | rahul@example.com
102         | priya@example.com
But in an enrollment table, one student can take many courses. Therefore, the combination of student_id and course_id may need to be unique rather than either column individually.
9. Multiple UNIQUE Constraints
A table can have multiple unique constraints.

CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    username VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE,
    phone VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE
);
This means:

• Each user_id must be unique.
  • Each username must satisfy its UNIQUE constraint.
  • Each email must satisfy its UNIQUE constraint.
  • Each phone must satisfy its UNIQUE constraint.
10. UNIQUE and Data Quality
Unique constraints can help prevent duplicate business identifiers from entering a relational table.

Incoming Data
      ↓
Check Unique Business Field
      ↓
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Already exists?     │
└──────────┬──────────┘
           ↓
     Yes       No
      ↓         ↓
  Reject /    Accept
  handle
      
Target Table
For example, a customer email may be required to be unique in an operational application.
11. UNIQUE in Data Engineering
Data Engineers frequently encounter uniqueness requirements when moving data between systems.
For example, suppose a source system says that customer_code identifies exactly one customer.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_code VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);
The unique constraint helps ensure that the target table does not contain multiple rows with the same customer code.
12. Detecting Duplicates Before Adding UNIQUE
If you want to add a UNIQUE constraint to an existing table, first check for duplicates.

SELECT
    email,
    COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
If this query returns rows, those values need to be investigated before adding the unique constraint.

Data Engineering Practice: Before adding a uniqueness constraint to an existing production table, profile the existing data and understand why duplicates exist. Do not simply delete duplicates without understanding their meaning.
13. `UNIQUE` Does Not Automatically Remove Duplicates
A UNIQUE constraint is a rule, not a deduplication operation.

Existing duplicate data
        ↓
UNIQUE constraint
        ↓
Constraint validation
        ↓
May fail if duplicates violate the rule
If duplicates already exist, adding the constraint can fail. You need a separate data-cleaning or reconciliation process.
14. UNIQUE vs `DISTINCT`
These concepts are different.

ConceptPurpose
UNIQUEEnforces a data integrity rule on a table
DISTINCTRemoves duplicate result rows from a query result
For example:

SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM employees;
This only changes the query result. It does not create a uniqueness rule on the table.
15. UNIQUE vs `GROUP BY`
GROUP BY groups rows for aggregation or grouped analysis. It does not enforce uniqueness on future data.

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
A UNIQUE constraint, on the other hand, is part of the table's integrity rules.
16. UNIQUE and Foreign Keys
A foreign key normally references a primary key or another eligible candidate key. A UNIQUE constraint can therefore sometimes define a key that another table references, depending on database rules.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_code VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE
);
The exact requirements for referencing a UNIQUE constraint vary by database system, so use the database documentation when implementing this design.
17. Removing a UNIQUE Constraint
A named UNIQUE constraint can generally be removed using ALTER TABLE.

ALTER TABLE customers
DROP CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email;
The exact syntax for dropping a unique constraint or its underlying index can vary by database.
18. Common Mistakes

• Thinking UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY are exactly the same.
  • Assuming UNIQUE allows or rejects NULL in the same way on every database.
  • Using UNIQUE when duplicate values are actually valid for the business.
  • Adding a UNIQUE constraint without checking existing duplicate data.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide duplicate data instead of fixing a data-quality problem.
  • Assuming a UNIQUE constraint automatically cleans existing duplicates.
  • Forgetting that composite UNIQUE constraints apply to the combination of columns.
  • Assuming a UNIQUE constraint automatically performs deduplication during ETL.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
UNIQUEPrevents duplicate values according to the constraint rules
Single-column UNIQUEOne column must satisfy uniqueness
Composite UNIQUEA combination of columns must be unique
Multiple UNIQUE constraintsA table can have multiple uniqueness rules
DISTINCTRemoves duplicate rows from a query result
Data EngineeringUseful for enforcing business-key uniqueness and data quality
Remember: PRIMARY KEY identifies each row. UNIQUE prevents duplicate values for a column or column combination that should be unique.
practice: Step 1: Create an employees table with a primary key and a UNIQUE email column.

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);
Step 2: Insert employees with different email addresses.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, email)
VALUES
    (101, 'Rahul', 'rahul@example.com'),
    (102, 'Priya', 'priya@example.com'),
    (103, 'Arun', 'arun@example.com');
Step 3: Try inserting another employee with an existing email address and observe the UNIQUE constraint violation.

INSERT INTO employees
    (employee_id, employee_name, email)
VALUES
    (104, 'Kiran', 'rahul@example.com');
Step 4: Create a users table with multiple UNIQUE constraints.

CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    username VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
